passages.quote: The velocity obeys the unforced viscosity-one Navier–Stokes momentum equation and has zero divergence.

comparisons.note: At viscosity one, the momentum and incompressibility conditions are exactly (1.1). Smoothness up to time zero and the initial value are also required, with the equations stated at positive times.

passages.quote: A profile solves the Navier–Stokes equation in similarity variables and repeats after one positive period up to an orthogonal spatial twist.

comparisons.note: The vanishing residual is ∂ₛW+W/2+(y·∇)W/2−ΔW+(W·∇)W+∇q=0, the momentum equation of (1.2). This expression contains neither the divergence condition nor the twisted recurrence in the rest of that display.

The premise includes the similarity equation, zero divergence and recurrence W(s+S,y)=RW(s,R⁻¹y) from (1.2). It also requires a smooth nonzero profile and uniform decay through two velocity derivatives and the pressure gradient, so the full premise demands more than this display.

passages.quote: The profile velocity and its spatial gradient decay uniformly at orders one and two in the inverse distance.

comparisons.note: The velocity and first-gradient bounds of (1.3) are included, with the same inverse-distance powers. The formal premise also requires |∇²W|≤C(1+|y|)⁻³ and |∇q|≤C(1+|y|)⁻³, so it demands more decay information.

This formula defines the physical curve from a similarity curve with final time one. The recurrence in (1.5) requires the separate period-and-twist assumption and is not asserted by this formula alone.

passages.quote: Rescaling a profile period to one introduces the coefficient 1/S in the time derivative of the similarity equation.

passages.quote: Two locally integrable fields agree modulo gradients when their difference pairs to zero with every smooth compactly supported divergence-free space-time test.

The statement specifies exactly the smooth compactly supported solenoidal test class. It does not itself assert that a difference of two fields pairs to zero.

passages.quote: Products of a smooth periodic time factor and a compactly supported solenoidal spatial field form a test family whose finite sums are dense in the solenoidal periodic space.

comparisons.note: The definition periodises an arbitrary compact space-time test by summing its integer translates. The displayed products a(θ)ψ(y) and their density require the additional separation argument.
The theorem proves that periodised compact solenoidal tests separate H_div. This is a density criterion for a related test family, while the phrase explicitly names separated products.

passages.quote: A unit-period perturbation is admissible when both its Laplacian and its full drift-time-diffusion operator are square integrable over a period.

comparisons.note: The formal conditions supply weak gradient and Hessian fields and the combined drift-time field separately, with finite period integrals for the gradient, Laplacian and drift-time field. The paper defines D_S directly by v ∈ L²_loc(R;X), Δv ∈ H and T_Sv ∈ H.
The result provides velocity and weak spatial derivatives with a square-integrable Hessian. It contains no time-drift condition, so it does not by itself give admissibility in D_S.

passages.quote: A prescribed symmetry combines a time shift with the corresponding orthogonal action on the velocity field, almost everywhere.

comparisons.note: The symmetry is v(θ + θ₀,Ry) = Rv(θ,y) almost everywhere. Substituting R⁻¹y gives exactly (7.5).

passages.quote: The paper sets m to two when the symmetry set contains a half-period shift and to one otherwise.

comparisons.note: The formal condition permits m = 1 whether or not a half-period symmetry exists, and permits m = 2 only when such a symmetry exists. The paper fixes m = 2 whenever that symmetry is available; choosing m = 1 uses the less favorable scalar budgets.

passages.quote: Every approximate profile obeys each prescribed space-time symmetry at every point.

comparisons.note: For every α ∈ K and every prescribed (R,θ₀), the approximate profile satisfies Wᵃ_α(θ + θ₀,Ry) = RWᵃ_α(θ,y) at every point, which is (7.7).

passages.quote: The approximate profile and its first spatial derivative have uniform inverse-radius decay of orders one and two.

comparisons.note: The formal decay condition includes the two bounds in (7.8) and also requires a chosen weak Hessian bounded by C_a(1 + |y|)⁻³. That extra requirement is absent from the displayed pair of inequalities.

passages.quote: The sum of squared period-space norms of the forcing fields is bounded by b_* squared.

comparisons.note: The forcing-field condition is Σ_i∫₀¹∫|b_i|² ≤ b_*², which is precisely the squared H-norm bound in (7.9).

passages.quote: The approximate profile solves the forced rescaled equation up to a square-integrable residual and a gradient.

comparisons.note: The residual is fixed explicitly by the approximate profile, weak Hessian, pressure-gradient representative and force. The paper allows any square-integrable representative of the same expression modulo gradients.

This is the differential expression including force and a supplied pressure-gradient field. Its square integrability and agreement modulo gradients are imposed by separate certificate conditions, so the definition alone does not state (7.10).

passages.quote: Each linear constraint pairs the perturbation gradient with a fixed matrix field over one period.

comparisons.note: The value is ∫₀¹∫∇v:Ξ_i, the linear constraint ℓ_i(v) in (7.11).

This quantity is the prescribed target for the perturbation, obtained by subtracting the approximate profile’s constraint from the target for the complete field. It is ℓ̄_i(α), rather than the functional ℓ_i(v) defined in the phrase.

passages.quote: The correction must solve the nonlinear forced perturbation equation and attain its prescribed linear constraints.

comparisons.note: The equation and constraints are imposed after Leray projection and v = T_S⁻¹f. The same conditions additionally require ‖(v,β)‖_{w,1} ≤ 2ε and ess sup‖∇v‖₂ ≤ M.

passages.quote: Linearised convection is the sum of advection of the perturbation by the approximate profile and advection of that profile by the perturbation.

comparisons.note: The expression sums Wᵃ_α,j ∂_jv and (∇Wᵃ_α)v, giving exactly the two terms of C_αv.

passages.quote: The correction is measured by its weighted gradient-plus-Laplacian energy, and the forcing coefficients add an omega-weighted Euclidean term.

comparisons.note: This is exactly the period energy ‖v‖²_w. The instantaneous energy and the forcing-coefficient term in the phrase are separate quantities.
This is exactly the instantaneous energy |u|²_w. Integration in time and the ω²|β|² term of the combined norm are not part of this definition.
The combined norm is √(‖v‖²_w + |β|²), so ω has already been reduced to one. The general weight in (7.14) is restored through a separate rescaling of the certificate.

passages.quote: The pointwise velocity estimate uses the constant c_w determined solely by the positive lower bound of the weight.

comparisons.note: For w_* > 0, the reciprocal square root simplifies to c_w = (4π√w_*)⁻¹ᐟ², exactly (7.15).

passages.quote: The reference-profile convection operator is obtained by linearising advection around the reference field.

comparisons.note: Taking W = Wʳ_α in (W·∇)v + (v·∇)W gives the reference convection Cʳ_αv of (7.16).

passages.quote: The residual seminorm collects finitely many orthogonal pairings and is bounded by c_0 times the full residual norm.

comparisons.note: The definition gives the weighted Euclidean norm of finitely many pairings. The inequality [F] ≤ c₀‖F‖_H requires orthonormality and weight bounds and is proved in the separate seminorm theorem.

passages.quote: The weighted correction and multiplier norm is controlled by the full reference residual norm, its finite-direction seminorm and the linear constraint values.

comparisons.note: The estimate has the same residual, row and constraint terms for the explicitly described weak perturbations. The formal certificate also requires c₂ ≥ 0, while §7.3 permits c₂ ∈ R.

passages.quote: The convection error from replacing the reference field by the approximate profile is at most c_r times the weighted correction norm.

passages.quote: The transfer loss is the convection gap multiplied by the sum of the full-residual and finite-direction constants.

passages.quote: The residual’s full norm and finite-direction seminorm have parameter-dependent bounds, with a common upper bound for the full norm.

comparisons.note: The certificate requires ‖Fᵃ_α‖_H ≤ δ(α) ≤ δ_max and [Fᵃ_α] ≤ δ₀(α), using squared integrals for the full norm and nonnegative bounds.

passages.quote: The combined residual and prescribed-constraint contribution fits within the transfer-adjusted radius epsilon.

The conclusion gives the free inverse and the averaged quadratic bound. The continuous representative and local energy identity in Lemma 7.4 are separate results.

The theorem gives symmetry preservation of the constructed inverse. It does not state bijectivity on D_S or the convergence assertions of Proposition 7.5.

passages.quote: The free evolution damps its gradient and Laplacian norms with exponential rates one quarter and three quarters.

comparisons.note: The operator norm estimate gives the gradient decay e⁻ˢ⁄⁴ in (7.47). It does not include the separate Laplacian estimate with decay e⁻³ˢ⁄⁴.

passages.quote: A weighted two-derivative energy controls the velocity supremum and gives the stated quadratic convection estimate over a period.

comparisons.note: The result gives the spatial product estimate (2π)⁻¹‖∇u‖₂‖Δu‖₂, which implies the weighted supremum bound. The quadratic estimate over a period is supplied by the other linked theorem.

passages.quote: The squared velocity supremum is bounded by c_w squared times the sum of the squared Laplacian L2 norm and w_* times the squared gradient L2 norm.

passages.quote: Linearised convection is bounded by the gradient norm, preserves symmetries and becomes compact after composition with the free inverse.

The result proves invariance of the projected convection and other projected terms. The norm bound and compactness assertion in Lemma 7.7 require separate theorems.
The result proves compactness of projected convection composed with the free inverse. The complete bound and unprojected symmetry statement in Lemma 7.7 are established elsewhere.

passages.quote: The two convection terms are controlled pointwise by the profile decay factors multiplying the perturbation gradient and velocity.

The paper displays a combined pointwise estimate in (7.50). This result bounds (v·∇)W in L² using the L³ norm of (1 + |y|)⁻² and the Sobolev embedding of v into L⁶.

passages.quote: Outside a ball, the convection norm is bounded by a tail coefficient tending to zero times the perturbation gradient norm.

comparisons.note: The bound ‖C_αv‖²_{L²(|y|>r)} ≤ C(1 + r)⁻¹‖∇v‖₂² gives an exterior coefficient tending to zero, which is exactly the qualitative assertion in this phrase.

passages.quote: The reference coercive estimate transfers to the approximate profile with its left side multiplied by one minus the transfer loss.

comparisons.note: The reduced certificate divides the residual and constraint constants by 1 − ϑ and replaces the reference field by the approximate field. This is exactly absorption of the convection gap in (7.52).

passages.quote: The linearised equation with forcing coefficients and matching linear constraints is uniquely solvable for every invariant projected right-hand side and constraint target.

comparisons.note: The theorem gives the inverse and injectivity after the substitution f = T_Sv and reduction to unit forcing weight, identical profiles and zero gap. The paper states the solve for the original certificate directly on D_S^Γ × Rⁿ.

passages.quote: The constrained linear map returns the projected linearised residual and the correction’s linear constraint vector.

passages.quote: Because the free part is solenoidal, projecting the full residual only projects convection and the forcing fields.

passages.quote: A solution of the linearised constrained equation has a uniform-in-time gradient estimate determined by its weighted energy, residual size, forcing size and available half-period symmetry.

passages.quote: The gradient supremum is controlled by weighted mean energy and the residual-forcing contribution, with the half-period improvement when available.

passages.quote: The mean upper bound for energy growth is at most the residual-plus-forcing norm times the correction norm, plus the frozen-form loss.

comparisons.note: The mean-growth estimate (7.56) is established within the proof. The returned conclusion is the resulting bound for the energy at each time, with coefficients 1/w_* + 2S c₃/m and 2S/m; the mean-growth estimate alone is not that conclusion.

passages.quote: For fixed parameter and quadratic input, the linear problem has right side minus the approximate residual minus that input and keeps the prescribed constraints.

comparisons.note: The right-hand side is −PFᵃ_α − P((v·∇)v), paired with the prescribed constraint target. Equation (7.57) allows an independent quadratic input g; this construction has already substituted the current correction into that input.
This definition gives the constrained linear operator in variables (f,β). The right-hand side −Fᵃ_α − g and the choice of prescribed constraints are supplied separately.

passages.quote: The projected approximate residual is invariant under the certificate symmetries and depends continuously on the parameter when paired with divergence-free tests.

comparisons.note: The conclusion includes invariance of the projected approximate residual. Testwise continuity in α is a separate theorem.
The conclusion gives testwise continuity of the projected residual and continuity of the correction target. Invariance is supplied by the other linked theorem.

passages.quote: Some admissible parameter has a nonlinear correction satisfying the two size bounds, the prescribed constraints and exact cancellation of the auxiliary force.

comparisons.note: The selected parameter and correction satisfy the two size bounds, constraints and zero total force after reduction of the certificate. The proof first solves each parameter by contraction and then finds a finite-dimensional zero; the paper uses a joint weak-topology fixed point.

For each fixed parameter, the result supplies the unique bounded nonlinear correction under the reduced certificate conditions. Selecting a parameter where its total force vanishes is a separate step.
The theorem proves a contraction for each fixed parameter. Existence of the correction and selection of a parameter with zero total force require additional fixed-point arguments.
The theorem proves continuity of the total multiplier map. It does not itself give a parameter where that map vanishes.

passages.quote: The selected nonlinear correction lies within the weighted radius 2 epsilon and gradient-supremum radius M.

comparisons.note: The conditions require the correction norm to be at most 2ε and the essential gradient supremum at most M, with forcing weight one after normalization.
The theorem says iteration preserves the two correction bounds. The existence of a selected correction satisfying them follows from the separate fixed-point theorem.

passages.quote: At the selected parameter, the correction multiplier exactly cancels the approximate forcing multiplier.

comparisons.note: The conclusion explicitly supplies α ∈ K and a bounded correction with βᵃ(α) + β = 0.

passages.quote: The corrected forcing multiplier satisfies the coordinate and complementary Euclidean enclosures that keep the parameter update inside K.

comparisons.note: The result proves the coordinate enclosure for j ∈ J. The complementary Euclidean enclosure is the other linked theorem.
The result proves the complementary squared Euclidean enclosure. The coordinate enclosures on J are supplied by the other linked theorem.

passages.quote: A nonzero periodic energy-space field with locally integrable similarity-equation terms, solving that equation modulo gradients, has a smooth decaying profile representative equal to the rescaled input field at every time.

comparisons.note: Proposition 7.11 preserves a specified weak field at every time while producing a smooth profile. This implication only asserts that existence of a weak recurrent field gives existence of a smooth recurrent profile; it permits an orthogonal twist and does not identify the output with the original field.

The result smooths a specified mild orbit and preserves that orbit at every time. The paper starts from a specified weak field and additionally obtains decay; those connecting steps are outside this result.
The result supplies existence of a recurrent mild orbit after the weak-equation steps. It does not yet return a smooth decaying representative identified with the specified weak field.
The result proves decay for an already smooth recurrent field satisfying an integral equation and additional bounds. Proposition 7.11 begins with a weak field and must first obtain that setting.

passages.quote: The smooth representative at similarity time s equals the original normalized-time field evaluated at s/S as an element of the homogeneous energy space.

comparisons.note: The result preserves a specified mild orbit at every time, almost everywhere in space. It does not identify that orbit with the original normalized-time weak field appearing in (7.62).

For a chosen orbit w, the assertion is equality of W(s) and w(s) almost everywhere in space for every s. With w(s) identified as the original field at s/S, this is precisely the equality in X in (7.62).
The conclusion asserts existence of a mild orbit. It does not retain the equality to the specified weak field that is required in (7.62).

passages.quote: The physical solution’s L6 norm, multiplied by the quarter-power of the remaining time, is uniformly bounded by periodicity of the normalized profile.

comparisons.note: The curve definition gives the physical-time rescaling. The exact L⁶ scaling, periodic boundedness and equality of the suprema in (7.63) are additional facts.

passages.quote: The physical velocity satisfies the Duhamel formula with the Leray heat kernel and the quadratic velocity tensor.

comparisons.note: The continuous Duhamel representative is a mild solution on each interior interval. Identifying the bilinear term with minus the differentiated Leray heat kernel gives (7.64).
The definition gives the heat-plus-bilinear expression on the right of (7.64). Equality to the actual solution and the identification of the bilinear kernel require separate results.

passages.quote: Heat-kernel bootstrapping bounds the physical velocity supremum by a constant times the inverse square root of the time to blow-up.

comparisons.note: The result gives a smooth recurrent field with uniform derivatives by a Sobolev and Picard argument. It does not state the displayed L⁶-to-L¹²-to-L∞ heat-kernel estimate with the factor (1 − t)⁻¹ᐟ².

passages.quote: The physical solution decays like the reciprocal of the sum of the diffusion length and the distance from the origin.

comparisons.note: The velocity decay yields the physical bound in (7.66) after rescaling, and the conclusion also includes derivatives and pressure-gradient decay. Its hypotheses already include a smooth integral-equation solution with uniform derivatives and a vanishing tail.
The velocity part is |W(s,y)| ≤ C/(1 + |y|), which rescales to (7.66). The same bound condition additionally controls first and second derivatives and the pressure gradient.

passages.section: B.1. The form of the data of a certificate
passages.quote: The prescribed spatial and temporal symmetries are a rotation by π/κ paired with a half-period time shift and a half-turn about the first axis paired with no time shift.

comparisons.note: The two required symmetries are the half-period twist by π/κ and the half-turn about the first axis. The auxiliary condition allows κ≥1; the cell assumptions impose the paper's κ≥3.
Every allowed symmetry is a power of the axial twist, possibly followed by the half-turn, with an integer time translation. This is the restriction on Γ stated after (B.1).
The cell assumptions require both symmetries and κ≥3, together with the entire cell, weight and matrix system. The phrase names only the two symmetry generators.

passages.section: B.1. The form of the data of a certificate
passages.quote: A lattice label ι determines a complex harmonic with time frequency 2ι₂−ι₁ and azimuthal frequency κι₁.

comparisons.note: The harmonic is exp(i[2π(2ι₂−ι₁)θ+κι₁φ]), with the same signs and integer frequencies as (B.2).
This supplies the pair of time and azimuthal frequencies (2ι₂−ι₁,κι₁). Forming the complex exponential of those frequencies is the remaining operation in (B.2).

passages.section: B.1. The form of the data of a certificate
passages.quote: The radial variable is compactified as |y|/(|y|+L), while the polar variable records the third coordinate divided by |y|.

comparisons.note: This defines only the compactified radius σ=|y|/(|y|+L). The polar coordinate η=y₃/|y| in (B.3) is defined separately.
This defines only η=y₃/|y| away from the origin. The compactified radius in (B.3) is a separate formula; the assigned value at the origin has no role in that coordinate description.

passages.section: B.1. The form of the data of a certificate
passages.quote: The weighted polar vector is η times the radial unit vector minus the vertical unit vector, and the weighted azimuthal vector is the cross product of the vertical and radial unit vectors.

comparisons.note: This defines the weighted polar vector p=ηy/|y|−e₃. The weighted azimuthal vector in (B.4) is a separate definition.
This defines the weighted azimuthal vector a=e₃×y/|y|. The weighted polar vector in (B.4) is a separate definition.

passages.section: B.1. The form of the data of a certificate
passages.quote: Each harmonic receives an integer multiple of a radial phase, and the radial differential operator acquires the corresponding imaginary phase-derivative term.

comparisons.note: This defines the oscillatory factor Eι exp(ilf(|y|²)). The radial differential operator Vₗ in (B.5) is supplied separately.
This defines Vₗ=σ(1−σ)∂σ+2il|y|²f′(|y|²). The oscillatory factor in (B.5) is a separate formula.
This supplies the scalar 2|y|²f′(|y|²), whose product with il is the phase contribution to Vₗ. The oscillatory factor and the remaining radial derivative in (B.5) are supplied separately.

passages.section: B.1. The form of the data of a certificate
passages.quote: A represented vector field is a finite harmonic sum whose three scalar coefficients multiply the radial, weighted polar and weighted azimuthal vectors.

comparisons.note: This is the finite complex sum of the individual vector harmonics. The real part in (B.6) is taken in the separate definition of the represented real field.
This defines one summand of (B.6), combining the radial, polar and azimuthal vectors with their three amplitudes. The sum over the finite harmonic set and its real part are separate operations.
The represented field is the real part of the finite vector-harmonic sum, as printed in (B.6). Conjugation, reflection and spline matching are required separately.
The condition imposes conjugation, reflection, spline matching and the exponent restrictions around (B.6). The displayed harmonic sum itself is a separate definition.

passages.section: B.1. The form of the data of a certificate
passages.quote: For nonzero azimuthal order, the radial and polar components contain prescribed origin, infinity and axis factors, and the azimuthal component is chosen to make the mode divergence free.

comparisons.note: The nonzero azimuthal mode uses the factors σʰ⁰(1−σ)ʰ(1−η²)² and division by κι₁ to enforce zero divergence. The zero azimuthal mode uses the stream and swirl formulas of (B.8).
This defines the phase-adjusted radial operator used in the divergence-free component formula. The three component amplitudes and their origin, decay and axis factors in (B.7) are separate.
Besides h₀≥2 and h≥1, the condition imposes the spline joins, conjugation and reflection needed for the represented field. These are additional requirements surrounding the formula (B.7).

passages.section: B.1. The form of the data of a certificate
passages.quote: For zero azimuthal order, a stream coefficient consisting of an origin term plus a spline and an independent swirl coefficient determine the three divergence-free components.

comparisons.note: The nonzero azimuthal mode uses the factors σʰ⁰(1−σ)ʰ(1−η²)² and division by κι₁ to enforce zero divergence. The zero azimuthal mode uses the stream and swirl formulas of (B.8).
This defines the stream coefficient Ψ=γg(σ)η+S. The factor σ(1−σ)ʰ and the derivatives that turn Ψ into the three components in (B.8) occur in the component formula.
Besides the zero-mode vanishing and spline conditions, the complete condition also handles nonzero modes and their symmetries. The formula (B.8) is one branch of the field construction.

passages.section: B.1. The form of the data of a certificate
passages.quote: The approximate profile is affine in the parameters through its mode coefficients, while its radial phase changes by a linear parameter rate times a cutoff logarithmic integral.

comparisons.note: This gives the affine combination of central and tangent fields at a fixed phase. The parameter-dependent phase change and its cutoff logarithmic integral in (B.9) are supplied separately.
This replaces the radial phase f by f+a f*. Taking a=k·α gives the phase substitution in (B.9), while the affine field combination and the construction of f* are separate.
This defines the scalar phase rate k·α. The affine field combination, shifted phase and cutoff integral in (B.9) require the other formulas.
This constructs f*(s) by the cutoff logarithmic integral up to √s, giving the printed integral at s=|y|². The affine field and parameter phase substitution in (B.9) are separate.

The profile representation is linked to its derivatives and to pinning values, with the target chosen to equal the approximate profile's pinning values. Consequently the correction has the zero pinning gap prescribed in Appendix B; the general certificate of Section 7 allows other gaps.

passages.section: B.1. The form of the data of a certificate
passages.quote: Each pinning functional pairs the perturbation gradient with a compactly supported tensor assembled from cell polynomials, harmonics and the reflection symmetry.

comparisons.note: The tensor Ξᵢ is assembled from the cell polynomials and their harmonics. Its pairing with the perturbation gradient gives the constraint in (B.10).

The cell tensor has the same harmonic and reflection construction as Ξᵢ, with matrix indices ordered as output then derivative direction. Transposing the paper's derivative-first convention identifies the same pairing in (B.10).
The functional is the integral over one period and space of the tensor inner product of ∇v and Ξᵢ. This is the pairing in (B.10).

passages.section: B.1. The form of the data of a certificate
passages.quote: The row fields are obtained by applying the inverse square root of their Gram matrix to the generators and then scaling each field to squared norm τₖ.

comparisons.note: This defines the Gram matrix G of the generators. The inverse square root, field combination and √τₖ scaling in (B.11) are separate operations.

This defines the mixing matrix G⁻¹ᐟ² for the admitted positive definite Gram matrix. The field combination and √τₖ scaling in (B.11) are supplied separately, with τₖ carried as a weight in the row seminorm.
The formal row fields have unit norm after multiplication by G⁻¹ᐟ². The paper includes √τₖ in eₖ itself; the same seminorm is recovered by multiplying the squared formal row pairing by τₖ.
The row weight is the cell test weight divided by c; at c=3/50 it is τₖ. The paper places √τₖ in the field eₖ, whereas the formal row seminorm carries τₖ as a separate weight.
The certificate uses orthonormal row fields and separate positive weights, including the bound τmax/c≤c₀². This gives the paper's weighted orthogonal rows after rescaling each field by √τₖ.
The theorem proves that the normalized rows have inner products δₖₗ. The paper's rows have squared norms τₖ, obtained by the additional √τₖ rescaling.

passages.quote: The ι-mode of a velocity field is its normalised time and azimuthal Fourier average after rotating the vector values back into a common frame.

comparisons.note: The projection averages over one time period and a full axial rotation, using the conjugate harmonic, inverse rotation of the vector values and the factor 1/(2π). These are precisely the operations in (B.12).
This only converts ι to the time and azimuthal frequencies used by the mode projection. The averaging, inverse rotation and normalization in (B.12) are in the separate projection formula.

passages.quote: A projected mode transforms under time translation and axial rotation by multiplication by its harmonic and rotation of its vector value.

comparisons.note: For periodic fields whose orbital integral exists, a time shift and axial rotation multiply the projected mode by its harmonic and rotate its vector value. This is (B.13), with the integrability needed for the change of variables stated explicitly.

passages.quote: The multiplier is characterised by its test pairing as the negative Laplacian plus harmonic skew terms weighted by the curl and velocity weights.

comparisons.note: The multiplier is characterized by the test pairing in (B.14), with finite L² norm, time periodicity and zero pairing against pressure gradients. These are the stated requirements that Mv belong to Hdiv.

passages.quote: The frequency seen in a frame rotating at νₚ is the physical time frequency plus νₚ times the azimuthal frequency.

comparisons.note: The rotating-frame frequency is 2πj/S+νj′. With (j,j′)=(2ι₂−ι₁,κι₁), this is exactly Ωₚ(ι) in (B.15).
The frequency pair is (2ι₂−ι₁,κι₁). The period scaling 2π/S and rotating-frame contribution νₚκι₁ in (B.15) are applied by the separate frequency formula.

passages.quote: The modal quadratic density is the sum of five coefficient-weighted squares of the Hessian, gradient of curl, curl, gradient and velocity.

comparisons.note: The five terms are the squares of the mode Hessian, curl gradient, curl, gradient and velocity with their respective coefficients. This matches (B.16), independently of the complete coefficient corrections that the paper leaves unwritten.

The five terms are the squares of the mode Hessian, curl gradient, curl, gradient and velocity with their respective coefficients. This matches (B.16), independently of the complete coefficient corrections that the paper leaves unwritten.

The five cell coefficients include the leading terms printed below (B.16) and the full multiplier corrections. The paper explicitly leaves those corrections unwritten, so their complete formulas cannot be compared term by term with the manuscript.

This gives the curl coefficient, including the positive λₚ|Ωₚ| contribution and the transport, rotation and coupling losses. The paper describes those losses after (B.16) without printing their complete formula.
This gives the gradient coefficient, including Zι−|∇²Dι|op−cw and the multiplier error terms. The full correction formula is absent from the paper's description of (B.16).

This gives the velocity coefficient, including −|∇²Zι|op, the positive (1−cμ)μₚ|Ωₚ| term and its error terms. The paper prints only this leading description, so full formula agreement remains uncheckable.

This is the amount removed from the curl-gradient coefficient by the multiplier estimates. The paper identifies that loss as part of the omitted corrections to (B.16), without giving its complete expression.

passages.quote: Reflecting the point and replacing ι by its reflected label preserves each coefficient of the modal density.

comparisons.note: The curl-coefficient reflection identity is proved for y₃≠0. The printed (B.17) gives no such exclusion; the excluded plane has zero measure for the density integrals.
The gradient-coefficient reflection identity is proved for y₃≠0. This is sufficient for the integrated symmetry argument, while the printed (B.17) is written without the pointwise restriction.
The velocity-coefficient reflection identity is proved for y₃≠0. The restriction leaves the integral unchanged but is narrower than the unrestricted pointwise wording of (B.17).
The curl-gradient allocation is invariant under the reflected label and point when y₃≠0. The printed coefficient identity does not state this restriction.

The weight and harmonic reflection conditions are explicit, while reflection of the auxiliary piecewise constant functions is required only off y₃=0. Thus the complete pointwise hypothesis differs from the unrestricted wording preceding (B.17).

The density reflection identity follows from the coefficient and derivative reflection identities at points with y₃≠0. It provides the almost-everywhere equality needed in the integrals, with a pointwise restriction absent from (B.17).

passages.quote: The stretching contribution combines the symmetric gradient of the reference flow acting on curl v with two terms coupling its vorticity gradient to v and ∇v.

comparisons.note: The stretching expression has the negative strain-curl square, the vorticity-gradient coupling and the final cross-product term with coefficient 1/2. Its signs and contractions agree with (B.18).

The stretching expression is (B.18), with a specified weak second derivative of the reference field used to form ∇curl Wʳ. For the admissible reference field this agrees almost everywhere with the paper's derivative.

passages.quote: The admissibility numbers bound the total curl weight, the total magnitude of its gradients and the squared velocity-weight sum relative to its frequency-weighted sum.

comparisons.note: The three inequalities (B.19) are included along with harmonic amplitude, transport and frequency requirements. This condition requires more data bounds than the displayed inequalities alone.

passages.quote: Admissible multiplier data give a finite μ-seminorm and an L² multiplier with the stated norm control, whose coercive pairing dominates the signed modal density whenever its negative part is finite.

comparisons.note: The multiplier theorem gives existence, finite μ-seminorm, the stated norm bound and a comparison of positive and negative density integrals under explicit weak derivative and coefficient assumptions. Finite negative density converts that comparison into (B.20); the paper leaves some admissibility conditions implicit.

This is the full multiplier assertion for weak perturbations, with positive and negative density integrals kept separate. It yields the real signed inequality of Proposition B.1 once the negative part is finite and the full coefficient assumptions hold.

Admissibility includes positive c,cμ<1, a positive period and lower weight, regularity and decay, transport and harmonic bounds, one-sided frequencies and all auxiliary losses. The paper describes several of these requirements without writing their complete formulas.

This specifies the test pairing, finite norm, periodicity and pressure orthogonality required of a multiplier. Proposition B.1 additionally asserts that such a multiplier exists and proves its norm and density bounds.

passages.quote: After subtracting the coercive energy, μ-seminorm and actuator terms, the multiplier pairing is at least the signed integral of the modal density and stretching term.

comparisons.note: This defines exactly the left side of (B.20), with c=3/50. It does not itself assert its lower bound by the signed density; that is the multiplier theorem.

This is the full multiplier assertion for weak perturbations, with positive and negative density integrals kept separate. It yields the real signed inequality of Proposition B.1 once the negative part is finite and the full coefficient assumptions hold.

The multiplier theorem gives existence, finite μ-seminorm, the stated norm bound and a comparison of positive and negative density integrals under explicit weak derivative and coefficient assumptions. Finite negative density converts that comparison into (B.20); the paper leaves some admissibility conditions implicit.

passages.quote: The integrated modal density is bounded below by 3/50 times ω²|β|², less the actuator pairing, 3/50 times the row seminorm squared and the pinning penalty 1000|ℓ(v)|².

comparisons.note: The condition states finiteness of negative density and the lower bound (B.21), with c and the pinning weight as parameters. Taking c=3/50 and the pinning weight 1000 gives the printed constants, after subtracting the finite negative integral.

The theorem derives the lower bound (B.21) and negative-part finiteness from the complete cell, shape and matrix conditions. Its assumptions include coefficient, gauge and error requirements that the paper explicitly leaves unwritten.
The condition fixes the constants c=3/50 and pinning weight 1000 and imposes the cell hypotheses used to derive (B.21). The density lower bound itself is a separate conclusion.

passages.quote: The multiplier norm, pinning weight and row-weight cap determine sufficient lower bounds on the certificate constants c₁, c₂ and c₀.

comparisons.note: The first two inequalities of (B.22) occur among the full cell-system conditions. Those conditions also impose the remaining certificate, matrix, profile and adjoint requirements.
The row condition gives τmax/c≤c₀², which becomes the third inequality of (B.22) at c=3/50. It contains neither the c₁ bound nor the c₂ bound.
The condition fixes c=3/50, the pinning weight 1000 and the row cap 400(1+2⁻¹⁸). The inequalities bounding c₁,c₂ and c₀ are imposed in the other certificate and row conditions.

passages.quote: The multiplier estimate and density lower bound imply the a priori certificate estimate for every admissible perturbation and right-hand side when c₁ and c₂ satisfy the stated budgets.

comparisons.note: The theorem proves the intermediate inequality obtained by adding (B.20) and (B.21). The c₁ and c₂ budgets and the scalar square-completion step are needed for Lemma B.2's final estimate (7.18).
The two density inequalities and the bounds c_M/√c≤c₁ and √(t/c)≤c₂ imply the a priori certificate estimate. With c=3/50 and t=1000, this is Lemma B.2 for the admitted weak perturbations.

passages.section: B.3. The cells, their complement and the tree
passages.quote: Reflection and rotation symmetries reduce the signed space-time density integral to 4π times its quarter-plane integral, with finiteness of positive and negative parts preserved.

comparisons.note: The positive and negative integrals each reduce by the factor 4π. These two identities give the signed identity and both finiteness conclusions stated in Lemma B.3.
The positive and negative integrals each reduce by the factor 4π. These two identities give the signed identity and both finiteness conclusions stated in Lemma B.3.

This is the general 4π change-of-variables identity for nonnegative, axially invariant families with the reflected-label symmetry. Applying it separately to the two signs of the density gives the signed statement of Lemma B.3.

The reflected velocity, gradient and Hessian mode identities supply the symmetry used in the quarter-plane reduction. The 4π integral identity and its finiteness conclusions are separate steps of Lemma B.3.

passages.section: B.3. The cells, their complement and the tree
passages.quote: The space-time integral of the modal density and stretching term equals 4π times the corresponding weighted quarter-plane integral.

comparisons.note: Both positive and negative density integrals satisfy their own 4π identity. The signed identity (B.23) follows when subtraction is defined, while the two nonnegative identities need no finiteness assumption.

Both positive and negative density integrals satisfy their own 4π identity. The signed identity (B.23) follows when subtraction is defined, while the two nonnegative identities need no finiteness assumption.

passages.section: B.3. The cells, their complement and the tree
passages.quote: Applying the reflection to a projected velocity mode is equivalent to projecting the reflected harmonic and reflecting its vector value.

comparisons.note: The reflected velocity-mode identity is proved almost everywhere for weak perturbations, together with the corresponding gradient and Hessian identities. The velocity clause is (B.24), interpreted in the weak-function setting of the surrounding argument.

passages.section: B.3. The cells, their complement and the tree
passages.quote: The stretching majorant charges curl energy, a gradient-velocity product and a split gradient/velocity square with the trace-free constant √(7/2).

comparisons.note: The majorant is s₁|curl G|²+√(7/2)s₂|G||v|+(1/2)√(7/2)s₃(h|G|²+|v|²/h), exactly (B.25).
This fixes the contraction constant to √(7/2), the constant in (B.25). It is the scalar used in that estimate, rather than the full stretching inequality.

passages.section: B.3. The cells, their complement and the tree
passages.quote: On compatible cell unknowns, the cell matrix minus its energy matrix is dominated by the retained potential and pairing forms, minus the top-degree form, plus eliminated-band and row contributions.

comparisons.note: The cell-matrix comparison is imposed on the allowed local vectors, with further eliminated-mode and row-matrix conditions. Identifying that set with the vectors XQxg also uses the pressure-gauge and compatibility conditions omitted from the paper.

A compatible local vector is a global row value plus pressure-gauge and constant-pressure directions, with real forcing and pinning coordinates. This is more explicit than the paper's notation x=XQxg, and the equivalence uses the additional gauge-invariance conditions.

passages.section: B.3. The cells, their complement and the tree
passages.quote: The high-degree gradient tail is absorbable up to I₂ times the sum of the cell’s radial factor times its minimum degree-(d+1) spectral eigenvalue and the angular gain (|κι₁|−2)₊²/r₂, with radial factor one on the axis.

comparisons.note: This supplies the spectral gain, including degree d+1, the axis-adjusted radial factor and the angular shift 2. The threshold (B.27) also multiplies that gain by the Hessian coefficient I₂, while absorption of the listed charges is a separate condition.

This supplies the spectral gain, including degree d+1, the axis-adjusted radial factor and the angular shift 2. The threshold (B.27) also multiplies that gain by the Hessian coefficient I₂, while absorption of the listed charges is a separate condition.
The radial factor is r₁ off the axis and 1 when r₁=0. This supplies precisely the axis convention in (B.27), while the eigenvalue and angular terms are supplied separately.

The complete absorption condition bounds the sum of gradient, potential, leakage and velocity-tail charges by I₂ times the gain in (B.27). The printed expression specifies the available threshold, without listing every charge in this condition.

passages.section: B.3. The cells, their complement and the tree
passages.quote: The unresolved-mode density subtracts the stretching majorant with the chosen constant and the additional curl, gradient and velocity charges from the original density.

comparisons.note: The unresolved density subtracts the stretching majorant and the curl, gradient and velocity charges before evaluating the mode. This is Iι° in (B.28).
This gives the coefficient changes caused by the stretching and curl, gradient and velocity charges. Evaluating the resulting coefficients on a mode gives the unresolved density in (B.28).

passages.section: B.3. The cells, their complement and the tree
passages.quote: The pointwise unresolved-mode test requires nonnegative Hessian weight, a permissible gradient split, nonnegative corrected velocity weight and a discriminant bound for the cross term.

comparisons.note: The condition is f₂≥0, 0≤t≤f₁*, f₀*≥0 and f₀₁²≤4(f₁*−t)f₀*. Splitting the middle inequality into two clauses does not change (B.29).
This defines the effective gradient coefficient f₁* used in (B.29). Nonnegativity of the other coefficients, the permissible split and the discriminant bound are separate parts of the test.

passages.section: B.3. The cells, their complement and the tree
passages.quote: An exterior region passes the scalar test when its inverse-square velocity and cross-term costs fit within the gradient floor at an allowed positive Hardy constant.

comparisons.note: The condition contains (B.30), its coefficient bounds and the two Hardy constants, with a measurable directional radius bounded above and bounded away from zero. Those radius bounds are not stated in the paper's description of an arbitrary direction-dependent exterior.
The directional radius is measurable, homogeneous of degree zero, uniformly positive and bounded above. The paper allows dependence on direction without spelling out these uniform bounds.

passages.section: B.3. The cells, their complement and the tree
passages.quote: On an admitted exterior region, the inverse-square weighted modal L² integral multiplied by Λ₀ is bounded by the modal gradient energy.

comparisons.note: The ray-exterior inequality uses the constant 1/4+(|κι₁|−1)₊² and the admitted weak modes. Its radius must be measurable, homogeneous, bounded above and bounded away from zero, assumptions absent from the printed geometric description.

For zero azimuthal frequency and the stated reflection symmetry, the square-exterior Hardy inequality has constant 2. Approximation extends the smooth component estimates to the weak modes used in (B.31).

This proves the smooth scalar component estimates with the required zero trace on the axis or reflection plane. The square-exterior inequality for weak vector modes in Proposition B.4 is obtained by a separate approximation and component assembly.
This specifies the admissible directional radius, including uniform positive lower and finite upper bounds. It is a geometric hypothesis for the ray Hardy theorem, rather than the inequality (B.31).

passages.section: B.3. The cells, their complement and the tree
passages.quote: Valid cell data yield finite negative density, the exterior stretching bound, compatible physical unknowns with the local and global error comparisons, and the square-exterior Hardy estimate with constant two.

comparisons.note: The conclusion is finiteness of the negative quarter-plane density for weak perturbations under coefficient lower bounds and reference-field regularity, without requiring the forcing equation. The 4π identity transfers it to I⁻; the remaining conclusions of Proposition B.4 are separate.

This proves only the almost-everywhere exterior stretching bound (B.32) within Proposition B.4. The negative-density, compatibility, cell-error and square-exterior conclusions require separate results.
The theorem expands the mean stretching term as a sum of harmonic couplings. The lower bound (B.32) then requires the trace-free contraction estimate and the prescribed majorants.

The result assembles compatible local and global unknowns and the cell estimates from the full finite-data conditions. The paper's four existential error numbers are replaced by explicit row, pairing, slack and credit contributions.

The theorem combines the resolved-mode energy estimate with an assumed residual-form bound to obtain the local cell inequality. Its conclusion uses explicit error contributions and signed parts, rather than the four existential numbers of (B.33).
This identifies the sum of the row contributions with the weighted row seminorm. The actuator, pinning and rectangle-credit contributions needed for the full bound (B.34) are handled separately.
This bounds the actuator and pinning pairings, including the errors of the surrogate profiles. The row seminorm and rectangle-credit parts of (B.34) are separate estimates.

This supplies the square-exterior Hardy conclusion with constant 2 for zero azimuthal modes and the required reflection. Negative-density finiteness and the cell and global error bounds of Proposition B.4 are separate results.

This proves the smooth scalar component estimates with the required zero trace on the axis or reflection plane. The square-exterior inequality for weak vector modes in Proposition B.4 is obtained by a separate approximation and component assembly.

passages.section: B.3. The cells, their complement and the tree
passages.quote: Almost everywhere outside the cells, the mean stretching term is at least minus the sum of the modal stretching majorants.

The theorem expands the mean stretching term as a sum of harmonic couplings. The lower bound (B.32) then requires the trace-free contraction estimate and the prescribed majorants.

passages.section: B.3. The cells, their complement and the tree
passages.quote: Each cell’s matrix value and unresolved-mode integral, after its credit term, are bounded by its integrated density plus row, pairing and multiplier error allowances.

comparisons.note: The local inequality uses explicit row, pairing, strain-slack and credit contributions and separates the positive and negative integrals. It serves the role of (B.33), with a specified symmetric pressure gradient and without the paper's four existential error variables.
The assertion requires that local comparison on every cell with its given matrix and error allocations. The paper expresses the same assembly stage through four real error numbers per cell.

The theorem combines the resolved-mode energy estimate with an assumed residual-form bound to obtain the local cell inequality. Its conclusion uses explicit error contributions and signed parts, rather than the four existential numbers of (B.33).

The result assembles compatible local and global unknowns and the cell estimates from the full finite-data conditions. The paper's four existential error numbers are replaced by explicit row, pairing, slack and credit contributions.

passages.section: B.3. The cells, their complement and the tree
passages.quote: Summed cell errors and plane-credit matrices are controlled by the row seminorm, actuator and pinning pairings, and the global multiplier-error allowance.

comparisons.note: This identifies the sum of the row contributions with the weighted row seminorm. The actuator, pinning and rectangle-credit contributions needed for the full bound (B.34) are handled separately.
This bounds the actuator and pinning pairings, including the errors of the surrogate profiles. The row seminorm and rectangle-credit parts of (B.34) are separate estimates.
This bounds the sum of the rectangle credits by the allocated mode energies. The row and actuator contributions are still needed to obtain the complete global error bound (B.34).
The global estimate already uses 2ζ·ℓ−|ζ|²/1000≤1000|ℓ|². It therefore bounds the assembled form by the final density gap, while (B.44) still displays the uncompleted pinning square.

passages.section: B.3. The cells, their complement and the tree
passages.quote: A mode with azimuthal frequency k obeys the four angular derivative bounds, which reduce its charged density to a two-variable quadratic form that is nonnegative under the scalar test.

comparisons.note: The four angular derivative inequalities in (B.35) are the first part of Lemma B.5. The coefficient reduction and the nonnegativity conclusion require the separate quadratic-form test.

This is the scalar positivity argument for five nonnegative derivative sizes satisfying the four angular inequalities and the coefficient test. Substituting the actual mode norms gives the last conclusion of Lemma B.5.
The theorem gives the final almost-everywhere nonnegativity conclusion of Lemma B.5. Its statement does not include the four angular bounds or the intermediate inequality (B.36).

The displayed conclusion replaces f₁*, f₀ and f₀₁ by an exterior lower gradient bound and inverse-square velocity and cross bounds. It is the subsequent exterior absorption estimate used in Lemma B.6, rather than the exact intermediate formula (B.36).

passages.section: B.3. The cells, their complement and the tree
passages.quote: Curl is bounded by √2 times the gradient, while shifted angular frequencies control velocity, gradient and curl through the next derivative and the cylindrical radius.

comparisons.note: The four inequalities are exactly the curl bound and the angular gains for velocity, gradient and curl printed in (B.35), interpreted almost everywhere for the weak modes.
The four inequalities are exactly the curl bound and the angular gains for velocity, gradient and curl printed in (B.35), interpreted almost everywhere for the weak modes.

passages.section: B.3. The cells, their complement and the tree
passages.quote: The charged density is bounded below by its effective gradient coefficient times |∇v̂|² plus its velocity coefficient times |v̂|² minus its cross coefficient times |∇v̂||v̂|.

comparisons.note: The displayed conclusion replaces f₁*, f₀ and f₀₁ by an exterior lower gradient bound and inverse-square velocity and cross bounds. It is the subsequent exterior absorption estimate used in Lemma B.6, rather than the exact intermediate formula (B.36).
This defines the coefficient f₁* in the lower bound (B.36), including both angular gains. The inequality for the full mode density is a separate result.

passages.section: B.3. The cells, their complement and the tree
passages.quote: A radial exterior satisfies the Hardy estimate with constant 1/4+(|κι₁|−1)₊², and admissible exterior coefficient bounds then make the integrated unresolved-mode density nonnegative with finite negative part.

comparisons.note: The ray-exterior inequality uses the constant 1/4+(|κι₁|−1)₊² and the admitted weak modes. Its radius must be measurable, homogeneous, bounded above and bounded away from zero, assumptions absent from the printed geometric description.

The theorem proves integrability of the negative exterior density and nonnegativity of its integral under the full exterior conditions. These include the bounded positive directional radius or the zero-mode square exterior, together with their coefficient budgets.
This is the complete exterior hypothesis, including its geometry, coefficient bounds and the scalar Hardy test. The conclusion that the exterior integral is nonnegative is a separate theorem.
The directional radius is measurable, homogeneous of degree zero, uniformly positive and bounded above. The paper allows dependence on direction without spelling out these uniform bounds.

passages.section: B.3. The cells, their complement and the tree
passages.quote: Integration by parts on a radial tail, followed by Cauchy–Schwarz, bounds the unweighted square integral by four times the radius-squared derivative integral.

comparisons.note: The theorem gives the final Hardy inequality in (B.37) for real C¹ functions of compact support and a>0. The boundary integration-by-parts identity and the complex-valued case are steps of the paper's argument, rather than this theorem's stated conclusion.

The conclusion is the spatial radial Hardy estimate for L⁶ fields with L² weak gradients on measurable ray exteriors. It extends the final estimate of (B.37) after integration over directions; it does not state the one-dimensional boundary identity.

passages.section: B.3. The cells, their complement and the tree
passages.quote: The global quadratic form is the sum of the global penalty, the embedded cell matrices and twice the embedded plane-credit matrices.

comparisons.note: The total quadratic form equals the global form plus the embedded cell forms and twice the rectangle-credit forms. The opposite-sign auxiliary forms cancel, giving (B.38).
The total matrix is defined as the sum of the attached matrices. Its identification with the global, cell and doubled credit terms of (B.38) is a separate equality.
This specifies the global, cell, cancelling and doubled credit forms attached to the tree. Their sum and its identification with the total form in (B.38) are separate operations.

passages.section: B.3. The cells, their complement and the tree
passages.quote: The node input is enclosed from below and its passed front from above by computed matrices with entrywise absolute-value error allowances.

comparisons.note: The real-node condition includes both comparisons in (B.39), the weighted residual test (B.40), symmetry, positive weights and the pivot slack bounds. Either displayed pair or row test alone is only part of that condition.

The complex-node condition includes the two comparisons and weighted residual test, together with the permitted complex coordinates, scale, pivot bounds and real and imaginary negative columns. These are the additional conditions described after (B.40).

passages.section: B.3. The cells, their complement and the tree
passages.quote: A weighted row sum of the absolute factorisation residual and both enclosure errors must fit within each node’s prescribed diagonal error radius.

comparisons.note: The real-node condition includes both comparisons in (B.39), the weighted residual test (B.40), symmetry, positive weights and the pivot slack bounds. Either displayed pair or row test alone is only part of that condition.

The complex-node condition includes the two comparisons and weighted residual test, together with the permitted complex coordinates, scale, pivot bounds and real and imaginary negative columns. These are the additional conditions described after (B.40).

passages.section: B.3. The cells, their complement and the tree
passages.quote: The tree conditions give a global lower bound by positive pivot slack minus squared negative-column pairings, and hence strict positivity on the subspace orthogonal to those columns.

comparisons.note: The theorem gives the global lower bound, including the root contribution. Strict positivity on the common column kernel additionally requires positive pivot coverage, established by the separate positive-subspace argument.

The conclusion gives a positive subspace of the root form with dimension at least the number of physical coordinates. The proof chooses the common kernel of negative-column pairings, while the printed lemma states positivity of the total form explicitly on that kernel.

This is the later finite-dimensional nonnegativity conclusion for a scalar quantity represented by a tree and state inequality. Lemma B.7 gives the tree lower bound and positivity on a subspace before that final step.

passages.section: B.3. The cells, their complement and the tree
passages.quote: The assembled global matrix dominates the sum of pivot-slack squares minus the sum of the squared negative-column pairings.

comparisons.note: The lower bound retains the quadratic form passed by the root, as well as the pivot gains and negative-column losses. The paper's (B.41) follows after dropping that nonnegative root contribution.
This defines the total matrix whose quadratic form is on the left of (B.41). The pivot-gain and negative-column lower bound is supplied by the tree theorem.

passages.section: B.3. The cells, their complement and the tree
passages.quote: At each tree node, the passed front plus pivot slack minus negative-column loss is bounded by the local leaf input and the fronts received from its children.

comparisons.note: The real-node enclosure and weighted row-sum bound imply that the local input dominates the outgoing form plus pivot gain minus negative-column loss. This is the real-node case of (B.42).
The complex-node enclosure gives the same inequality after conversion to real coordinates and splitting each negative column into real and imaginary parts. This is the complex-node case of (B.42).

The theorem derives a quadratic-form bound from the weighted absolute row-sum test for symmetric matrices. The input and outgoing enclosure errors of (B.39) must also be inserted to obtain the node inequality (B.42).
This concludes the global nonnegativity implication after all nodes and the state bound are assembled. The local inequality (B.42) is proved by the real- and complex-node enclosure results.

passages.section: B.3. The cells, their complement and the tree
passages.quote: The global matrix is required to be no larger than the negative multiplier and pinning diagonal penalty, with the global error allowance added to the multiplier coefficient.

comparisons.note: The global-form inequality is the bound (B.43), with additional compatibility of coordinates, pressure-gauge directions, free coordinates and the zero state. Thus this complete condition requires more than the displayed global matrix bound alone.
This defines the negative multiplier and pinning penalty on the right of (B.43), with c=3/50 and pinning weight 1000. The comparison of the global matrix with that penalty is imposed separately.

passages.section: B.3. The cells, their complement and the tree
passages.quote: If all the Appendix B cell conditions hold, the negative modal density is finite and the density lower bound (B.21) holds uniformly over the parameter box for every admissible perturbation, multiplier vector and right-hand side.

The tree theorem supplies the final algebraic nonnegativity step. The construction of compatible cell values, the density identity and negative-part finiteness are required to obtain Proposition B.8.

The result assembles compatible local and global unknowns and the cell estimates from the full finite-data conditions. The paper's four existential error numbers are replaced by explicit row, pairing, slack and credit contributions.

passages.section: B.3. The cells, their complement and the tree
passages.quote: After summing the cell bounds and cancelling local errors, 4π times the global quadratic value is bounded by the total density minus the multiplier gap, plus forcing, row and affine pinning terms.

The identity identifies the assembled tree form with the global, cell and credit forms. It does not assert the density upper bound or the pinning terms of (B.44).

passages.section: B.4. The other conditions and the statement

The inequality is written with sixth power integral raised to 1/3 and the gradient energy. At C=4/3 it is the square of the Sobolev inequality (B.45).

passages.section: B.4. The other conditions and the statement
passages.quote: The weighted energy controls the gradient, Laplacian, their product and the supremum norm through the weight lower bound and the constant c_w.

comparisons.note: These estimates control spatial supremum norms and period gradient energy for weak fields with constant weight. They supply the bounds needed from (B.46), without asserting its entire four-inequality display for an arbitrary variable weight.

The combined assertion consists of spatial supremum and period energy estimates at constant weight. The paper's (B.46) is a four-part spatial statement assuming only a lower bound for a possibly variable weight.

The inequality is the scalar step combining the gradient and Laplacian energies to obtain the supremum bound with its Fourier constant. It is neither the full energy estimate (B.46) nor its three other conclusions.

passages.section: B.4. The other conditions and the statement
passages.quote: Central and boxwise profile norm bounds satisfying the scalar budgets yield the gap-transfer estimate and a lower frozen-form bound with c₃ at least the sum of its reference and shift contributions.

comparisons.note: This bounds the L² difference between the linearized convection operators by the weighted perturbation energy. The reference-form and profile-form bounds are separate parts of Lemma B.9.

This bounds from below the change in the quadratic form when the reference profile is replaced by the approximate profile. The operator-difference and reference-form bounds are separate parts of Lemma B.9.

This bounds the reference quadratic form from below by a constant times the spatial energy, using the convection identity. The operator-difference and profile-form bounds are separate parts of Lemma B.9.

These are the four profile-difference norm bounds and their gap and form-shift budgets. The implication from these and the reference bounds to the joint conclusions of Lemma B.9 is supplied by separate estimates.
These are the reference-gradient, strain and scalar-budget hypotheses used in Lemma B.9. The lemma also needs the profile-difference estimates and the implications to its two final bounds.

passages.section: B.4. The other conditions and the statement

This gives the reference L³ gradient norm and strain lower bound. The four difference norms in (B.47) are separate conditions.

passages.section: B.4. The other conditions and the statement
passages.quote: The central and box errors are allocated to the gap and form-shift constants, while the reference strain and gradient costs are allocated to the reference form constant.

This contains the middle budget of (B.48), bounding the reference-form coefficient c₃′. The cr and c₃″ budgets for profile differences are separate.

passages.section: B.4. The other conditions and the statement
passages.quote: The transport error is bounded by a supremum norm for the advecting difference, an L² gradient norm times the velocity supremum for the central difference, and an L³ gradient norm times the velocity L⁶ norm for the box difference.

This proves the two estimates using an L² or L³ gradient of the coefficient field. The supremum estimate for the advecting field is the separate first line of (B.49).
Hölder's inequality and ‖u‖L⁶≤(2/√3)‖∇u‖L² give the L³ coefficient product bound. This supplies the Sobolev step in the last line of (B.49).

passages.section: B.4. The other conditions and the statement
passages.quote: Either the stated L³ bound or the stated L² bound on an adjoint field implies the quadratic adjoint pairing estimate after applying its corresponding weight-dependent conversion factor.

comparisons.note: Integrating the quadratic adjoint slice estimate over one period gives (7.32) with either norm choice of Lemma B.10. The formulation also permits the adjoint to depend on the parameter.

The theorem gives the almost-everywhere time-slice estimate for (v·∇)v paired with ψ, using either its L² or L³ norm. The period-integrated conclusion of Lemma B.10 is supplied by a separate integration step.

This states the sufficient L² or L³ adjoint norm hypothesis, including its coefficient bound. The implication to the integrated pairing estimate (7.32) is supplied by the separate quadratic-adjoint theorem.
The coefficient is 2/(√3w*) for the L³ choice and c_w/√w* for the L² choice. These are the two constants of Lemma B.10; the adjoint norm and the resulting pairing estimate are separate.

passages.section: B.4. The other conditions and the statement
passages.quote: A field with the prescribed dual bound has an integrable pairing with every period-one field locally square-integrable in time with values in the energy space X, and the pairing is bounded by the dual number times its gradient norm.

The statement permits tests without time periodicity and does not itself assert the joint absolute integrability printed in Lemma B.11.
The weighted Hardy bound 2‖|y|R′‖H≤n′ gives the dual estimate for the plain remainder. The finite harmonic remainder and their sum are separate parts of Lemma B.11.

This proves the dual estimate for the finite harmonic remainder with coefficient (|k|+1/2)⁻² and the component weights 1/2,1/2,1. The plain remainder is combined with it in the full estimate of Lemma B.11.

This requires a decomposition into a finite harmonic remainder and a plain remainder, with the sum of their bounds at most the prescribed total. Lemma B.11 additionally deduces integrability and the dual pairing estimate.

This requires the finite harmonic expansion, distinct component and frequency labels, and the weighted inverse-square amplitude bound. Lemma B.11 additionally combines this part with the plain remainder to obtain the dual estimate.
This requires the weighted L² bound 2‖|y|R′‖H≤n′ for the plain remainder. The finite harmonic contribution and their combined dual estimate are separate parts of Lemma B.11.

passages.section: B.4. The other conditions and the statement
passages.quote: An azimuthal scalar mode of order k satisfies the inverse-square Hardy bound with coefficient (|k|+1/2)².

comparisons.note: The sharp constant (|k|+1/2)² is proved for a smooth compactly supported scalar mode. Equation (B.50) is stated for the L⁶ mode with an L² weak gradient, obtained by a separate approximation argument.

The weak extension controls a sum of projected modes using the sharp inverse-square factors and the total gradient energy. It supplies the weak estimate needed for (B.50), with approximation and orthogonality stated as inputs rather than a single arbitrary-mode conclusion.
This gives the dual pairing estimate for a finite harmonic residual, using the sharp Hardy inequality and orthogonality. Its conclusion differs from the single-mode inverse-square inequality (B.50).
This assumes the finite harmonic residual budget with the sharp inverse-square denominator. It uses (B.50) in the dual-pairing estimate, rather than asserting that Hardy inequality itself.

passages.section: B.4. The other conditions and the statement
passages.quote: The auxiliary potentials have the stated inverse-power value and gradient decay, while their weak Laplacians, flux divergence and pressure gradient satisfy a common bound of order |y|⁻¹(1+|y|)⁻².

comparisons.note: The potential assumptions add |U|≲(1+|y|)⁻¹ and require bounded-near-origin Laplacians with decay (1+|y|)⁻⁴ for G and (1+|y|)⁻³ for U. These imply the coarser common derivative bound (B.51), after increasing its unspecified constant.

The theorem obtains the stronger potential decay and weak derivatives from explicit finite-series, axis and joining conditions. The paper leaves this potential representation unwritten, so only its analytic consequences can be compared directly with (B.51).

The result establishes the scalar, flux, pressure and compact-generator regularity facts for the finite potential representation. These provide the analytic inputs to Lemma B.12; the paper omits the detailed representation conditions.

The condition imposes polynomial joining, axis behavior and endpoint decay for the finite potential series. The paper explicitly does not print that representation, so this condition cannot be identified with the displayed analytic bounds (B.51) alone.

passages.section: B.4. The other conditions and the statement
passages.quote: The adjoint remainder is the central-period formal adjoint applied to ψⱼ, corrected by the pin-generator Laplacians, pressure gradient, two potential Laplacians and the flux divergence.

comparisons.note: The residual combines the adjoint transport, negative divergence of the pin flux, ∇q, ∆G+w*∆U and −div Fᵀ. With divergence-free pin generators and the stated transpose convention, this is (B.52).
The expression is −S(0)⁻¹∂θψ−ψ−(y·∇)ψ/2 minus reference advection plus its transposed gradient action. The Laplacian, pins and potential corrections required by (B.52) are supplied separately.
The flux is ∇ψ−ΣYⱼₗ(∇Φ̃ₗ−∇Φ̃ₗᵀ). For divergence-free generators its negative divergence gives −∆ψ+ΣYⱼₗ∆Φ̃ₗ, identifying the corresponding terms of (B.52).
This is the adjoint transport evaluated at the central period and central profile. The Laplacian, pin flux and potential corrections of Rⱼ,α in (B.52) are not part of this expression.
These identifications choose the fixed adjoint, central field, tangent fields and period coefficients used in the residual construction. The formula for Rⱼ,α in (B.52) is formed separately from them.

The assumptions identify the potential series and pin fields with the certificate and require their full finite-data validity. The detailed potential representation is omitted from the paper, so its complete hypothesis cannot be compared from (B.52) alone.

The compact pin generators must satisfy the explicit spline, support, axis and mesh conditions. These supply the divergence-free compact fields used in (B.52), with more representation detail than its displayed residual.

The definition constructs Φₗ from cylindrical cell data and Φ̃ₗ from the compact harmonic representation. Their regularity, support and divergence conditions are separate assumptions used to justify (B.52).

These are the regularity, decay, symmetry, divergence and expansion facts for the harmonic field construction. They justify the use of the compact pin generators in (B.52), rather than stating its residual formula.
The theorem proves those harmonic-field regularity, decay, divergence and support facts. They justify the identity div(∇Φ̃−∇Φ̃ᵀ)=∆Φ̃ used in (B.52), but do not themselves state the residual equality.

passages.section: B.4. The other conditions and the statement
passages.quote: The potential, parameter-variation, time-frequency and pin-approximation budgets in (B.53) imply the linear adjoint defect estimate uniformly on the parameter box.

comparisons.note: The linear adjoint estimate follows from the representation, potential, dual, pin-error and parameter-shift estimates, under explicit potential and curl-potential hypotheses. For the cell construction these are supplied by the finite shape conditions, and the empty fitted set recovers Lemma B.12.
This is the list of the norm, dual, parameter and pin-error hypotheses, together with their budget. Lemma B.12 additionally concludes the pairing estimate from those hypotheses.

The identifications specialize the general adjoint construction to the paper's central and tangent fields and an empty fitted set. They supply the correct data for Lemma B.12, without asserting its pairing bound.

The theorem supplies the weak derivatives, decay and compact pin properties of the actual potential data from the full cell conditions. The remaining representation and numerical estimates are needed for Lemma B.12.

The result establishes the scalar, flux, pressure and compact-generator regularity facts for the finite potential representation. These provide the analytic inputs to Lemma B.12; the paper omits the detailed representation conditions.

The pairing identity is obtained from an explicit decaying curl potential and a solenoidal test approximation. Taking zero reference advection gives (B.54); the general identity includes reference convection.

The theorem approximates the time-cutoff adjoint field by compact solenoidal tests in the required spatial and time-derivative norms. This justifies the integration by parts in (B.54), before the numerical bound of Lemma B.12.

The theorem bounds the combined residual and flux pairing by the potential budget times ‖v‖w. It gives the first contribution to (B.53), with the parameter-shift and pin-error contributions supplied separately.

This gives the dual estimate for the decomposed remainder, including its stated spatial and time integrability. The potential, parameter-variation and pin-approximation contributions are still needed for Lemma B.12.
The weighted Hardy bound 2‖|y|R′‖H≤n′ gives the dual estimate for the plain remainder. The finite harmonic remainder and their sum are separate parts of Lemma B.11.

This proves the dual estimate for the finite harmonic remainder with coefficient (|k|+1/2)⁻² and the component weights 1/2,1/2,1. The plain remainder is combined with it in the full estimate of Lemma B.11.
Replacing the pin tensors by compact solenoidal generators costs at most (nΦ+nYcΞ/√w*)‖v‖w. This is the final contribution to (B.53).

Weighted Cauchy–Schwarz bounds the sum of the free parameter advection terms by the coordinate-radius factor times nv+nd. The period shift and pinning terms are added in the full estimate of Lemma B.12.

passages.section: B.4. The other conditions and the statement
passages.quote: The square-root potential defect, weighted parameter and time-frequency costs, and pin-approximation error must sum to at most the chosen linear adjoint error aⱼ.

comparisons.note: The condition includes the total budget (B.53), its norm and dual hypotheses, and additional fitted-direction terms in the general case. The paper's expression is recovered when the fitted set is empty.

The sum includes the potential budget, possible fitted-direction budgets and the free parameter and time-shift budgets. Setting the fitted set empty and adding the separate pin charge gives the three-part expression (B.53).
The pin charge is nΦ+nYcΞ/√w*, exactly the last part of (B.53). The potential and parameter-shift terms are in the separate defect budget.
The links set the fitted-direction set empty, which removes those additional terms from the general budget. They identify the data but do not state the numerical inequality (B.53).

passages.section: B.4. The other conditions and the statement
passages.quote: Pairing the self-similar linear operator with ψ transfers time differentiation and dilation to ψ and leaves the spatial diffusion term as a gradient pairing.

comparisons.note: The pairing identity is obtained from an explicit decaying curl potential and a solenoidal test approximation. Taking zero reference advection gives (B.54); the general identity includes reference convection.

The general identity pairs a perturbation equation including reference convection against a decaying adjoint field with a curl potential. Setting the reference field to zero gives the free-operator identity (B.54).

The theorem approximates the time-cutoff adjoint field by compact solenoidal tests in the required spatial and time-derivative norms. This justifies the integration by parts in (B.54), before the numerical bound of Lemma B.12.
This defines the adjoint transport expression that appears after integration by parts. The equality of period-space pairings in (B.54) is a separate statement.

passages.section: B.4. The other conditions and the statement
passages.quote: A velocity with square-integrable weak gradient can be paired with a matrix divergence by moving the derivative onto the velocity and reversing the sign, under the stated integrability assumptions.

comparisons.note: The identity assumes L² matrix columns and |y| times their divergence in L². The paper states (B.55) for matrix fields with divergence in L⁶ᐟ⁵; these are different sufficient hypotheses, and the formal argument uses the weighted Hardy bound.

The integration-by-parts identity is proved for fluxes with decay |F| and |y| |div Fᵀ|≲(1+|y|)⁻ᵃ, a>3/2. This covers the potential fluxes used here, with a narrower decay-based hypothesis than the printed general statement (B.55).

This is the distributional divergence condition tested against compactly supported smooth scalar functions. Extending it to the energy-space field v in (B.55) requires the additional integrability and approximation argument.

passages.section: B.4. The other conditions and the statement
passages.quote: The linear adjoint defect splits into a potential-remainder pairing, parameter and period-variation pairings, and the two pin-approximation errors.
