Breakdown.AdjointDefect.AdjointDefectEnt.text: The sum includes the potential budget, possible fitted-direction budgets and the free parameter and time-shift budgets. Setting the fitted set empty and adding the separate pin charge gives the three-part expression (B.53).
The flux is ∇ψ−ΣYⱼₗ(∇Φ̃ₗ−∇Φ̃ₗᵀ). For divergence-free generators its negative divergence gives −∆ψ+ΣYⱼₗ∆Φ̃ₗ, identifying the corresponding terms of (B.52).

Breakdown.AdjointDefect.AzimuthalBounded.text: The harmonic part has distinct component, time-frequency and azimuthal-frequency triples and the weighted sum with denominator (|k|+1/2)². This is exactly the improved harmonic budget in the definition preceding Lemma B.11.

Breakdown.AdjointDefect.Internal.Potenti.text: The identity assumes L² matrix columns and |y| times their divergence in L². The paper states (B.55) for matrix fields with divergence in L⁶ᐟ⁵; these are different sufficient hypotheses, and the formal argument uses the weighted Hardy bound.

Breakdown.AdjointDefect.IsPotentialData.text: The potential assumptions add $|U|\lesssim(1+|y|)^{-1}$ and require bounded-near-origin Laplacians with decay $(1+|y|)^{-4}$ for $G$ and $(1+|y|)^{-3}$ for $U$. These imply the coarser common derivative bound (B.51), after increasing its unspecified constant.

Breakdown.AdjointDefect.adjointDefectBri.text: The theorem combines the potential, parameter and pin estimates after decomposing the adjoint pairing. It concludes the absolute bound (7.33); the raw three-line equality (B.56) is established through separate identities inside that argument.

Breakdown.AdjointDefect.remainderField.text: The residual combines the adjoint transport, negative divergence of the pin flux, ∇q, ∆G+w*∆U and −div Fᵀ. With divergence-free pin generators and the stated transpose convention, this is (B.52).

Breakdown.CellCert.GivenFields.heightRat.text: For y≠0 the polar coordinate is y₃/|y|. A value is also assigned at y=0, where the polar coordinate in the paper is undefined; none of the geometric formulas needs that point.

Breakdown.CellLayerSystem.CellSystemCond.text: The fifteen groups of assumptions include multiplier bounds, pointwise cell inequalities, matrix comparisons, and profile, potential, adjoint and offset conditions. They supply the full hypothesis of the certificate construction, including the requirements omitted after Proposition B.14; their satisfaction by concrete data remains an assumption.

Breakdown.CellLayerSystem.isExtendedCert.text: The construction produces a certificate after choosing a sufficiently large decay constant, from the full fifteen groups of cell assumptions and the analytic estimates. The paper omits some finite-data hypotheses, so equivalence of the complete condition lists cannot be checked from Proposition B.14 alone.

Breakdown.CellLayerSystem.spaceBreakdown.text: The conclusion is whole-space nonexistence of a global smooth solution with uniformly bounded energy, obtained by composing the cell and profile implications. Proposition B.14 itself concludes that the data form a certificate; the existence of valid concrete data remains an assumption here.

Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.Is.text: The profile representation is linked to its derivatives and to pinning values, with the target chosen to equal the approximate profile's pinning values. Consequently the correction has the zero pinning gap prescribed in Appendix B; the general certificate of Section 7 allows other gaps.

Breakdown.Cert.Internal.FreePerturbation.text: The free similarity equation is verified by differentiating its pairing with smooth compactly supported test fields.

Breakdown.Cert.bordered.text: The unknown is $f = T_S v$; applying the free inverse recovers $v$ before convection and the constraints are evaluated.

Breakdown.Cert.extendedDataContinuityHol.text: Continuity is proved after testing the residual against solenoidal fields. No continuity of the unprojected residual in H is assumed.

Breakdown.Cert.extendedFrozenBridgeHolds.text: The lower bound at the approximate profile is obtained by adding the reference-profile lower bound and the allowed shift of the quadratic form.

Breakdown.Cert.freeEnergyLocalHolds_of.text: The energy identity is integrated over time intervals for a continuous periodic scalar energy. The physical-time identity (7.45) is related by the similarity change of variables.

Breakdown.Cert.productBoundHolds_of.text: The estimate allows different first and second factors, using the weighted norm of the first and the gradient supremum of the second.

Breakdown.Cert.sizeZ.text: At this stage ω has been reduced to one by rescaling the forcing fields and their coefficients.

Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.EliminationC.text: The cell-matrix comparison is imposed on the allowed local vectors, with further eliminated-mode and row-matrix conditions. Identifying that set with the vectors XQxg also uses the pressure-gauge and compatibility conditions omitted from the paper.

Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.InRowRange.text: A compatible local vector is a global row value plus pressure-gauge and constant-pressure directions, with real forcing and pinning coordinates. This is more explicit than the paper's notation x=XQxg, and the equivalence uses the additional gauge-invariance conditions.

Breakdown.CertCell.Bridge.Internal.ModeT.text: The gradient-coefficient reflection identity is proved for y₃≠0. This is sufficient for the integrated symmetry argument, while the printed (B.17) is written without the pointwise restriction.
The curl-coefficient reflection identity is proved for y₃≠0. The printed (B.17) gives no such exclusion; the excluded plane has zero measure for the density integrals.
The velocity-coefficient reflection identity is proved for y₃≠0. The restriction leaves the integral unchanged but is narrower than the unrestricted pointwise wording of (B.17).
The curl-gradient allocation is invariant under the reflected label and point when y₃≠0. The printed coefficient identity does not state this restriction.

Breakdown.CertCell.Bridge.IsFlipCompatib.text: The weight and harmonic reflection conditions are explicit, while reflection of the auxiliary piecewise constant functions is required only off y₃=0. Thus the complete pointwise hypothesis differs from the unrestricted wording preceding (B.17).

Breakdown.CertCell.Bridge.IsModeClass.text: The two required symmetries are the half-period twist by π/κ and the half-turn about the first axis. The auxiliary condition allows κ≥1; the cell assumptions impose the paper's κ≥3.

Breakdown.CertCell.Bridge.modeFlip.text: The reflected velocity-mode identity is proved almost everywhere for weak perturbations, together with the corresponding gradient and Hessian identities. The velocity clause is (B.24), interpreted in the weak-function setting of the surrounding argument.

Breakdown.CertCell.Bridge.modeShiftRotat.text: For periodic fields whose orbital integral exists, a time shift and axial rotation multiply the projected mode by its harmonic and rotate its vector value. This is (B.13), with the integrability needed for the change of variables stated explicitly.

Breakdown.CertCell.Bridge.modeTermFlip.text: The density reflection identity follows from the coefficient and derivative reflection identities at points with y₃≠0. It provides the almost-everywhere equality needed in the integrals, with a pointwise restriction absent from (B.17).

Breakdown.CertCell.CellCalculus.IsCellFo.text: The local inequality uses explicit row, pairing, strain-slack and credit contributions and separates the positive and negative integrals. It serves the role of (B.33), with a specified symmetric pressure gradient and without the paper's four existential error variables.

Breakdown.CertCell.CellHypothesis.text: The full cell assumptions include $\kappa\ge 3$ and the constants $w^*=39/50$, $c=3/50$, pinning weight $1000$ and row cap $400(1+2^{-18})$. They also require the cell, matrix, pressure and error conditions described, and partly omitted, in Appendix B.

Breakdown.CertCell.CellMatField.field.text: The cell tensor has the same harmonic and reflection construction as Ξᵢ, with matrix indices ordered as output then derivative direction. Transposing the paper's derivative-first convention identifies the same pairing in (B.10).

Breakdown.CertCell.Certificate.PassesCom.text: The complex-node condition includes the two comparisons and weighted residual test, together with the permitted complex coordinates, scale, pivot bounds and real and imaginary negative columns. These are the additional conditions described after (B.40).

Breakdown.CertCell.GivenShape.IsTimeFiel.text: These are the conjugation, reflection, spline joining, vanishing and exponent conditions around (B.6)–(B.8). They specify admissible coefficients; the vector-field formula itself is supplied separately.

Breakdown.CertCell.GivenShape.reducedCom.text: The nonzero azimuthal mode uses the factors σʰ⁰(1−σ)ʰ(1−η²)² and division by κι₁ to enforce zero divergence. The zero azimuthal mode uses the stream and swirl formulas of (B.8).

Breakdown.CertCell.GivenShape.shapeInfoF.text: The represented field is the real part of the finite vector-harmonic sum, as printed in (B.6). Conjugation, reflection and spline matching are required separately.

Breakdown.CertCell.Instance.GeneratedByC.text: Every allowed symmetry is a power of the axial twist, possibly followed by the half-turn, with an integer time translation. This is the restriction on Γ stated after (B.1).

Breakdown.CertCell.ModeCoefficients.ofPi.text: The five cell coefficients include the leading terms printed below (B.16) and the full multiplier corrections. The paper explicitly leaves those corrections unwritten, so their complete formulas cannot be compared term by term with the manuscript.

Breakdown.CertCell.RowValues.mix.text: For positive definite Gram data the mixing matrix is $G^{-1/2}$. The factor $\sqrt{\tau_k}$ is applied through the separate row weight when the row seminorm is formed.

Breakdown.CertCell.RowValues.rowFieldOf.text: The formal row fields have unit norm after multiplication by $G^{-1/2}$. The paper includes $\sqrt{\tau_k}$ in $e_k$ itself; the same seminorm is recovered by multiplying the squared formal row pairing by $\tau_k$.

Breakdown.CertCell.RowValues.rowWeightOf.text: The row weight is the cell test weight divided by $c$; at $c=3/50$ it is $\tau_k$. The paper places $\sqrt{\tau_k}$ in the field $e_k$, whereas the formal row seminorm carries $\tau_k$ as a separate weight.

Breakdown.CertCell.TailBand.IsDirectionR.text: The directional radius is measurable, homogeneous of degree zero, uniformly positive and bounded above. The paper allows dependence on direction without spelling out these uniform bounds.

Breakdown.CertCell.TailBand.TailBudget.H.text: The complete absorption condition bounds the sum of gradient, potential, leakage and velocity-tail charges by I₂ times the gain in (B.27). The printed expression specifies the available threshold, without listing every charge in this condition.

Breakdown.CertCell.initialState_closed.text: The global estimate already uses 2ζ·ℓ−|ζ|²/1000≤1000|ℓ|². It therefore bounds the assembled form by the final density gap, while (B.44) still displays the uncompleted pinning square.

Breakdown.CertCell.labelPhase.text: The harmonic is exp(i[2π(2ι₂−ι₁)θ+κι₁φ]), with the same signs and integer frequencies as (B.2).

Breakdown.CertReduction.EnergyBoundsHold.text: The combined assertion consists of spatial supremum and period energy estimates at constant weight. The paper's (B.46) is a four-part spatial statement assuming only a lower bound for a possibly variable weight.

Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.IsAdmissibleWeak.text: Admissibility includes positive c,cμ<1, a positive period and lower weight, regularity and decay, transport and harmonic bounds, one-sided frequencies and all auxiliary losses. The paper describes several of these requirements without writing their complete formulas.

Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.PieceMultiplierDe.text: This is the full multiplier assertion for weak perturbations, with positive and negative density integrals kept separate. It yields the real signed inequality of Proposition B.1 once the negative part is finite and the full coefficient assumptions hold.

Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.RowRestClause.text: The condition states finiteness of negative density and the lower bound (B.21), with c and the pinning weight as parameters. Taking c=3/50 and the pinning weight 1000 gives the printed constants, after subtracting the finite negative integral.

Breakdown.DichotomyHolds.text: For a compact perturbation of an operator of norm at most b≤α<β, the spectral conclusion gives a commuting finite-rank projection and geometric bounds with α<r₁<r₂<β, together with surjectivity on the exceptional range. Taking α=b=exp(−S/4), β=1 and r₁<Θ<r₂ gives the two convergent series in (4.11).

Breakdown.ExtendedCertificateData.IsHeld.text: A fixed-parameter correction must satisfy the equation, constraints, weighted radius and essential gradient-supremum bound.

Breakdown.ExtendedCertificateData.defect.text: A weak Hessian and a pressure-gradient representative are selected when the residual field is formed.

Breakdown.ExtendedCertificateData.params.text: Intervals constrain the adjoint coordinates; a scaled Euclidean ball constrains the complementary coordinates.

Breakdown.ExtendedCertificateData.target.text: Subtract the approximate profile’s constraint from the complete-field target to obtain the prescribed correction target ℓ̄(α).

Breakdown.FarField.farFieldDecay_holds.text: Weighted estimates for the profile integral equation give velocity derivatives through order two and pressure-gradient decay.

Breakdown.FarField.periodicLerayProfileE.text: The input and output assert existence. The conclusion does not preserve an equality with a specified original weak field.

Breakdown.FarField.smoothFieldOfOrbit_ho.text: The smooth velocity preserves the chosen mild orbit at every time, with equality almost everywhere in space.

Breakdown.Freq.BilinCompact.text: For positive heat time, the operator in the second input is compact when its first input is a compact smooth solenoidal field in the dense test class. Lemma 3.2 allows every first input in X; extending to that class uses density and continuity in operator norm.

Breakdown.Freq.IsWeakSolution.text: The weak momentum identity is imposed at interior times against compact solenoidal test fields, with diffusion written by the gradient pairing and transport by the advection pairing. The full assumptions also require smooth decaying slices, continuity in X, L²-continuous differences between slices, and continuity of test pairings at the endpoints.

Breakdown.Freq.bilinX.text: The bilinear operator on X is specified by its dual trilinear pairing, with the transport formula then proved on a dense compact test class. Display (2.3) defines it through projected heat evolution for all inputs in X.

Breakdown.Freq.heatDivFree.text: The projected heat map takes L² forcing into the gradient-weighted Fourier realization of X. The formula in (2.2) is stated on the larger class L¹+L².

Breakdown.HeatBilinear.text: The heat operators form a strongly continuous contraction semigroup, and the symmetric bilinear kernel commutes with forward heat shifts. Its $\tau^{-3/4}$ bound is required only for $0<\tau\le 1$, whereas (3.12) requires that bound for every $\tau>0$.

Breakdown.Held.testSetZero_of.text: The proof forms the simplified Newton update and uses the two enclosures to keep it in K; a fixed point then has zero total force.

Breakdown.IsPerturbation.text: The drift-time field is $S^{-1}\partial_\theta v + \frac{1}{2}v + \frac{1}{2}(y\cdot\nabla)v$. The Laplacian is subtracted separately in the equation.

Breakdown.IsRightSide.text: The relation is equality of integrals against all smooth compactly supported solenoidal space-time tests.

Breakdown.IsSimilarityProfile.text: The velocity and pressure solve the smooth similarity equation, with $|\nabla^j W| \le C(1+|y|)^{-1-j}$ for $j=0,1,2$ and $|\nabla q| \le C(1+|y|)^{-3}$. Periodicity and nonvanishing are separate assumptions when this local profile condition is used.

Breakdown.IsSmoothSolution.text: The velocity and pressure are smooth on nonnegative times, the prescribed initial velocity is attained, and the momentum equation and zero divergence hold at positive times. Setting the viscosity to one gives (1.1).

Breakdown.MildFramework.text: The assumptions require the short-time bilinear bound with exponent −3/4, the heat and dilation identities, and compactness when one bilinear input ranges over a dense set. Rotation compatibility is imposed separately in the physical realization.

Breakdown.MildFramework.IsOrbit.text: A continuous nonzero energy-space curve has positive period P, obeys w(s+P)=ρw(s), and solves the similarity-time integral equation. The physical-time identities (1.5) and (4.2) require the change of variables and dilation as well.

Breakdown.MildRegular.text: From compact smooth solenoidal initial data, a mild curve on [0,T] has smooth velocity and pressure representatives, with bounded kinetic energy and gradient norm on that interval. Lemma 2.3 additionally states energy nonincrease throughout the lifespan and a periodic assertion.

Breakdown.MonodromyStatement.text: After sufficiently short intervals are composed and the twist removed, the period map differs compactly from the free product, whose norm is at most exp(−P/4). The same statement also provides inverses of the short-interval operators with norm at most 4/3.

Breakdown.Periodic.HeatDivFreeComparison.text: Compactly supported $L^2$ forcing has arbitrarily small local projected-heat discrepancy, measured by $\delta$ times its $L^{3/2}$ norm, at sufficiently small scale and on a compact positive-time window. Lemma 6.1 gives an all-time $CL^{-7/2}$ estimate for the divergence of a $W^{1,1}$ tensor, in terms of that tensor’s $L^1$ norm.

Breakdown.Periodic.KernelSharpBound.text: The bilinear smoothing bound is $C\tau^{-3/4}$ in the inhomogeneous unit-torus norm, for $0<\tau\le 1$. Lemma 3.7 and (3.20) use mean-zero homogeneous spaces at every spatial period and all positive times.

Breakdown.Periodic.TorusBlowup.text: The conclusion supplies a smooth periodic solenoidal datum and a mild trajectory whose inhomogeneous H¹ norm is unbounded on [0,T), for some T>0. Proposition 2.2 additionally gives T≤1, the two-sided rate, and local convergence to the profile.

Breakdown.Periodic.TransplantNorm.text: The rescaled transplant has squared norm ∫|∇g|²+μ∫|g|² because the unit-torus norm is inhomogeneous. The equality in (6.1) concerns the homogeneous gradient norm, preserved by unscaled periodization.

Breakdown.Periodic.V.text: The unit-torus Fourier norm uses 1+4π²|k|² and permits the zero mode. Displays (3.15) and (3.16) concern the homogeneous gradient norm on mean-zero fields, with a separate equivalence to H¹ at period one.

Breakdown.PeriodicSimilarityProfileExist.text: A smooth nonzero profile has a positive period and an orthogonal twist, solves the similarity equation, and satisfies uniform bounds $|\nabla^j W| \le C(1+|y|)^{-1-j}$ for $j=0,1,2$ and $|\nabla q| \le C(1+|y|)^{-3}$. The second-derivative and pressure-gradient bounds are additional written hypotheses beyond (1.3).

Breakdown.PieceWeights.IsMultiplierField.text: The multiplier is characterized by the test pairing in (B.14), with finite L² norm, time periodicity and zero pairing against pressure gradients. These are the stated requirements that Mv belong to Hdiv.

Breakdown.PotentialShape.IsPotentialSeri.text: The condition imposes polynomial joining, axis behavior and endpoint decay for the finite potential series. The paper explicitly does not print that representation, so this condition cannot be identified with the displayed analytic bounds (B.51) alone.

Breakdown.Realization.text: The physical representation preserves the gradient norm, nonvanishing, rotations and dilations. It also converts the stated distributional evolution into a mild solution and supplies dense smooth compactly supported solenoidal data.

Breakdown.TransferHolds.text: For every prescribed dense class of initial data and every ε>0, the formal conclusion chooses one mild solution whose datum is within ε of W(0) and whose dilated error is at most C(1−t)^κ for some κ>0. Proposition 2.1 also chooses a fixed finite-dimensional correction space and treats every sufficiently close datum; that whole family is absent from this conclusion.

Breakdown.WeakProfile.physicalCurve.text: The formula uses s = s₀ − log(1−t) and dilation by 1/(1−t); conversion from normalized time θ to s has already occurred.

Breakdown.WeakProfile.physicalIdentity_o.text: The theorem transforms the weak nonlinear equation after testing. The paper also interprets the separate free-operator identities (7.41) distributionally.

Breakdown.extended_certificate_orbit_pro.text: The proof assembles the analytic implications, while its conclusion retains only existence of a weak profile. The parameter and quantitative bounds are not part of that conclusion.

Breakdown.physicalField.text: The physical curve is $D_{(1-t)^{-1}}W(s_0-\log(1-t))$, with final time fixed to one and arbitrary phase $s_0$. Display (1.4) allows any positive final time $T$.

Breakdown.rowNorm.text: The weights of orthonormal row fields can be absorbed into the fields to recover the paper’s orthogonal family.

Breakdown.sigmaSimilarityIntegrand.text: Solenoidal tests remove pressure, and integration by parts transfers the derivatives to the test field.

Breakdown.Freq.heat_holds.text: The heat flow is a strongly continuous contraction semigroup from time zero, is self-adjoint, and agrees with its Gaussian Fourier multiplier. Its realization on X supplies (3.3).

Breakdown.Periodic.trigHs.text: Finite Fourier polynomials on the unit cell satisfy an L⁶ estimate using the weight 1+4π²|k|². Display (3.18) is the homogeneous Sobolev inequality for all mean-zero fields, uniformly over every period; (3.19) is a separate heat-forcing estimate.

Breakdown.Cert.Internal.FreeEnergyLocal..text: The theorem constructs a continuous periodic energy-space representative of the free solution and its similarity-time integrated energy identity.

Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.ce.text: The constant residual has the similarity drift, diffusion, central advection, actuator force and $\nabla(q^0-|W_0^0|^2/2)$. These are exactly $F^{(0)}$ in (B.57).

Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.li.text: The linear residual includes the period derivative ςᵢ∂θW₀⁰, both mixed advections, the tangent actuator force and ∇(qⁱ−W₀⁰·W₀ⁱ). This is F⁽ⁱ⁾ in (B.57).

Breakdown.AdjointDefect.AdjointDefectBou.text: The condition collects all potential, remainder, parameter and pin-error bounds and their final sum. It allows fitted directions; after setting that set empty, its numerical budget is (B.53), while the implication to (7.33) is a separate theorem.

Breakdown.AdjointDefect.AdjointDefectEnt.text: This is the adjoint transport evaluated at the central period and central profile. The Laplacian, pin flux and potential corrections of Rⱼ,α in (B.52) are not part of this expression.

The sum includes the potential budget, possible fitted-direction budgets and the free parameter and time-shift budgets. Setting the fitted set empty and adding the separate pin charge gives the three-part expression (B.53).
The pin charge is $n\Phi+nYc\Xi/\sqrt{w^*}$, exactly the last part of (B.53). The potential and parameter-shift terms are in the separate defect budget.
The flux is ∇ψ−ΣYⱼₗ(∇Φ̃ₗ−∇Φ̃ₗᵀ). For divergence-free generators its negative divergence gives −∆ψ+ΣYⱼₗ∆Φ̃ₗ, identifying the corresponding terms of (B.52).

Breakdown.AdjointDefect.AzimuthalBounded.text: The harmonic part has distinct component, time-frequency and azimuthal-frequency triples and the weighted sum with denominator (|k|+1/2)². This is exactly the improved harmonic budget in the definition preceding Lemma B.11.

Breakdown.AdjointDefect.AzimuthalParts.m.text: The weak extension controls a sum of projected modes using the sharp inverse-square factors and the total gradient energy. It supplies the weak estimate needed for (B.50), with approximation and orthogonality stated as inputs rather than a single arbitrary-mode conclusion.

Breakdown.AdjointDefect.AzimuthalParts.s.text: The sharp constant (|k|+1/2)² is proved for a smooth compactly supported scalar mode. Equation (B.50) is stated for the L⁶ mode with an L² weak gradient, obtained by a separate approximation argument.

Breakdown.AdjointDefect.DualBounded.text: The remainder is a sum of a plain weighted L² part and a finite harmonic part, with nonnegative budgets whose sum is at most n. This is the dual-bound definition preceding Lemma B.11.

Breakdown.AdjointDefect.Internal.Potenti.text: The integration-by-parts identity is proved for fluxes with decay |F| and |y| |div Fᵀ|≲(1+|y|)⁻ᵃ, a>3/2. This covers the potential fluxes used here, with a narrower decay-based hypothesis than the printed general statement (B.55).
The identity rewrites the residual and flux pairing as the remainder pairing minus ⟨∆v,G⟩ plus ⟨∇v,w*∇U−F⟩. It is the potential part of (B.56), with the parameter and pin terms supplied separately.

The identity assumes L² matrix columns and |y| times their divergence in L². The paper states (B.55) for matrix fields with divergence in L⁶ᐟ⁵; these are different sufficient hypotheses, and the formal argument uses the weighted Hardy bound.

Breakdown.AdjointDefect.Internal.transpo.text: The identity separates the central adjoint transport, fitted and free profile shifts, and inverse-period shifts. It supplies the parameter part of (B.56), before integration and addition of the potential and pin contributions.

Breakdown.AdjointDefect.IsPotentialData.text: The potential assumptions add $|U|\lesssim(1+|y|)^{-1}$ and require bounded-near-origin Laplacians with decay $(1+|y|)^{-4}$ for $G$ and $(1+|y|)^{-3}$ for $U$. These imply the coarser common derivative bound (B.51), after increasing its unspecified constant.

Breakdown.AdjointDefect.IsWeakMatrixDive.text: This is the distributional divergence condition tested against compactly supported smooth scalar functions. Extending it to the energy-space field v in (B.55) requires the additional integrability and approximation argument.

Breakdown.AdjointDefect.RemainderBounded.text: The plain remainder condition is ‖|y|R′‖H²≤(n′/2)² with n′≥0. It is equivalent to the first part of the paper's dual-bound definition.

Breakdown.AdjointDefect.RepresentationHo.text: The general identity pairs a perturbation equation including reference convection against a decaying adjoint field with a curl potential. Setting the reference field to zero gives the free-operator identity (B.54).

Breakdown.AdjointDefect.adjointDefectBri.text: The theorem combines the potential, parameter and pin estimates after decomposing the adjoint pairing. It concludes the absolute bound (7.33); the raw three-line equality (B.56) is established through separate identities inside that argument.

The linear adjoint estimate follows from the representation, potential, dual, pin-error and parameter-shift estimates, under explicit potential and curl-potential hypotheses. For the cell construction these are supplied by the finite shape conditions, and the empty fitted set recovers Lemma B.12.

Breakdown.AdjointDefect.adjointTransport.text: The expression is $-S(0)^{-1}\partial_\theta\psi-\psi-(y\cdot\nabla)\psi/2$ minus reference advection plus its transposed gradient action. The Laplacian, pins and potential corrections required by (B.52) are supplied separately.

Breakdown.AdjointDefect.dualBoundedBound.text: The two parts of the dual decomposition imply the absolute pairing bound and spatial integrability at almost every time, with integrability of the time integral. The statement permits tests without time periodicity and does not itself assert the joint absolute integrability printed in Lemma B.11.

Breakdown.AdjointDefect.freeShiftBoundHo.text: Weighted Cauchy–Schwarz bounds the sum of the free parameter advection terms by the coordinate-radius factor times nv+nd. The period shift and pinning terms are added in the full estimate of Lemma B.12.

Breakdown.AdjointDefect.pinChargeHolds_p.text: Replacing the pin tensors by compact solenoidal generators costs at most $(n\Phi+nYc\Xi/\sqrt{w^*})\lVert v\rVert_w$. This is the final contribution to (B.53).

Breakdown.AdjointDefect.potentialBoundHo.text: The theorem bounds the combined residual and flux pairing by the potential budget times ‖v‖w. It gives the first contribution to (B.53), with the parameter-shift and pin-error contributions supplied separately.

Breakdown.AdjointDefect.remainderAzimuth.text: This proves the dual estimate for the finite harmonic remainder with coefficient $(|k|+1/2)^{-2}$ and the component weights $1/2,1/2,1$. The plain remainder is combined with it in the full estimate of Lemma B.11.

Breakdown.AdjointDefect.remainderField.text: The residual combines the adjoint transport, negative divergence of the pin flux, ∇q, ∆G+w*∆U and −div Fᵀ. With divergence-free pin generators and the stated transpose convention, this is (B.52).

Breakdown.AdjointDefect.remainderPlainHo.text: The weighted Hardy bound 2‖|y|R′‖H≤n′ gives the dual estimate for the plain remainder. The finite harmonic remainder and their sum are separate parts of Lemma B.11.

Breakdown.AdjointDefect.representationHo.text: The pairing identity is obtained from an explicit decaying curl potential and a solenoidal test approximation. Taking zero reference advection gives (B.54); the general identity includes reference convection.

Breakdown.AdjointDefect.testFieldDensity.text: The theorem approximates the time-cutoff adjoint field by compact solenoidal tests in the required spatial and time-derivative norms. This justifies the integration by parts in (B.54), before the numerical bound of Lemma B.12.

Breakdown.Periodic.R3Factor.text: With one compact smooth solenoidal input, the whole-space bilinear interaction factors through the velocity and gradient restricted to its support ball. Time integration and assembly produce the first factorization in (6.9).

Breakdown.Periodic.RightInversePerturb.text: If A has a right inverse R with ‖R‖≤K and ‖A′−A‖K≤1/2, then A′ has a right inverse of norm at most 2K. This supplies the inverse-correction step used after (6.16); it is independent of the three separate choices of the torus period in that display.

Breakdown.Periodic.SeqPerturbation.text: For normalized time intervals, a right inverse and $64\lVert R\rVert^2 C_K L^{1/4}(\rho+\lVert\xi\rVert)\le 1$ give exact mild intervals with matching endpoints. Both the datum correction and each normalized error are bounded by $2\lVert R\rVert(\rho+\lVert\xi\rVert)$, while Lemma 4.8 uses the $C^\kappa$ norm of the combined forcing $e^{t\Delta}\chi-F^a$.

Breakdown.Periodic.ShellInverseTransfer.text: Two localized comparisons within $\delta$ and an explicit smallness inequality transfer a bounded whole-space right inverse to an exact periodic right inverse. Lemma 6.3 first constructs a particular approximate inverse with a defect of order $L^{-1/2}$.

Breakdown.Periodic.TorusBlowup.text: The conclusion supplies a smooth periodic solenoidal datum and a mild trajectory whose inhomogeneous H¹ norm is unbounded on [0,T), for some T>0. Proposition 2.2 additionally gives T≤1, the two-sided rate, and local convergence to the profile.

Breakdown.Periodic.TorusChainEq.text: Factoring the periodic interaction through the local restriction gives the periodic linearized sequence operator. The particular discrepancy ζ−z restricted to the ball in (6.13) is not part of this identity.

Breakdown.Periodic.TorusFactor.text: For a compact smooth solenoidal input transplanted at an admissible scale, the periodic bilinear interaction factors through the rescaled local restriction. This is the local ingredient of the second global time-integrated identity in (6.9).

Breakdown.Periodic.TransplantNorm.text: The rescaled transplant has squared norm ∫|∇g|²+μ∫|g|² because the unit-torus norm is inhomogeneous. The equality in (6.1) concerns the homogeneous gradient norm, preserved by unscaled periodization.

Breakdown.Periodic.TransplantSmooth.text: A compact smooth solenoidal field transplanted at an admissible scale becomes smooth, periodic and solenoidal, and agrees with its scaled copy near the cell centre. This statement does not assert preservation of the homogeneous norm or zero spatial mean.

Breakdown.Periodic.TrigHs.text: Finite Fourier polynomials on the unit cell satisfy an L⁶ estimate using the weight 1+4π²|k|². Display (3.18) is the homogeneous Sobolev inequality for all mean-zero fields, uniformly over every period; (3.19) is a separate heat-forcing estimate.

Breakdown.Periodic.V.text: The unit-torus Fourier norm uses 1+4π²|k|² and permits the zero mode. Displays (3.15) and (3.16) concern the homogeneous gradient norm on mean-zero fields, with a separate equivalence to H¹ at period one.

Breakdown.Periodic.approxFieldProperties.text: The smooth solenoidal cutoff has fixed support around the centre of the unit torus and agrees exactly with the physical profile on a fixed inner ball. Lemma 5.1 uses an arbitrary radius r and additionally gives explicit gradient-error and mass estimates.

Breakdown.Periodic.approxResidualSmall.text: For the normalized $n$th approximate interval, the residual is bounded by $\theta^n KT^{1/4}$, assuming the profile bounds and $\lambda^{1/4}<\theta$. Lemma 6.2 instead states a global $C^\kappa$ residual bound of order $L^{-1/2}$ on the large torus.

Breakdown.Periodic.approxSizes.text: For sufficiently small positive final time, the normalized approximate intervals have a uniform upper bound and pointwise lower norm bound c/2. This does not itself assert a norm identity under periodization or a rate for the corrected trajectory.

Breakdown.Periodic.breakdownOnTorus_of_p.text: The paper constructs the periodic trajectory and estimates (1.7); the formal conclusion gives, for every positive viscosity, smooth periodic solenoidal data admitting no global smooth solution with periodic velocity, with no periodicity restriction on its pressure. The premise includes additional profile decay, while the rate and the local comparison on $B_{1/16}$ are absent from this conclusion.

Breakdown.Periodic.chainOp.text: The operator subtracts the previous-interval shift, the initial-data contribution, and interaction followed by local restriction from the trajectory. This factorization organizes the inverse transfer; the exact defect formula of (6.13) involves the paper’s particular candidate inverse.

Breakdown.Periodic.comparisonSmall.text: For any δ>0, the localized interaction and initial-data maps on the unit torus are within δ of their whole-space counterparts when the scale is sufficiently small. The statement gives no explicit power of the large period L in (6.11) or (6.15).

Breakdown.Periodic.cutoffDivergenceFree.text: Multiplying the homotopy potential by a smooth cutoff and taking its curl produces a smooth solenoidal field. Specializing to χ(x)=η(x/r) gives the incompressibility used after (5.1).

Breakdown.Periodic.cutoffField.text: The cutoff is χg+∇χ×A, the product-rule expression for curl(χA) when curl A=g. With χ(x)=η(x/r) and centre zero it is the field in (5.1).

Breakdown.Periodic.cutoffGradientClose.text: For any ε>0, the squared gradient error of the rescaled cutoff is at most ε when T−t is sufficiently small. Displays (5.2) and (6.4) specify an explicit inverse-square-root radius bound, which is absent from this conclusion.

Breakdown.Periodic.cutoffMassBound.text: The rescaled cutoff has squared $L^2$ mass at most $K/\sqrt{T-t}$ for $0<T-t\le 1$. Reading this as the radius estimate in (5.2) requires undoing the spatial rescaling and taking a square root.

Breakdown.Periodic.freeHeatComparison.text: For each compact smooth solenoidal datum, the rescaled torus and whole-space free heat flows converge uniformly on a bounded nonnegative time interval as the scale tends to zero. Display (6.3) gives the explicit all-positive-time error $CL^{-5/2}\lVert f\rVert_{L^1}$.

Breakdown.Periodic.glueUnbounded.text: A uniformly positive approximate norm and a bounded correction multiplied by θⁿ, with 0<θ<1, make the joined physical trajectory unbounded before its positive final time. The conclusion does not contain the all-time two-sided rate or the local comparison in (1.7).

Breakdown.Periodic.heatDivFreeComparison.text: Compactly supported $L^2$ forcing has arbitrarily small local projected-heat discrepancy, measured by $\delta$ times its $L^{3/2}$ norm, at sufficiently small scale and on a compact positive-time window. Lemma 6.1 gives an all-time $CL^{-7/2}$ estimate for the divergence of a $W^{1,1}$ tensor, in terms of that tensor’s $L^1$ norm.

Breakdown.Periodic.homotopyCurl.text: For any smooth solenoidal g and centre x₀, this smooth homotopy potential has curl g. The proof of (5.1) uses the centre-zero case.

Breakdown.Periodic.homotopyPotential.text: The potential integrates σg(x₀+σ(x−x₀))×(x−x₀) from zero to one. At x₀=0 this is the vector potential A in (5.1).

Breakdown.Periodic.kernel.text: The periodic symmetric bilinear term is constructed from Fourier coefficients on the unit torus with its inhomogeneous H¹ norm. Display (3.17) gives the projected-transport formula in the mean-zero homogeneous spaces of arbitrary period.

Breakdown.Periodic.kernelSharpBound.text: The bilinear smoothing bound is $C\tau^{-3/4}$ in the inhomogeneous unit-torus norm, for $0<\tau\le 1$. Lemma 3.7 and (3.20) use mean-zero homogeneous spaces at every spatial period and all positive times.

Breakdown.Periodic.operatorNormBounds_ho.text: The localized interaction and restriction maps are bounded in the supremum norms of the rescaled interval sequences, and the sequence shifts have norm at most λ¹⁄⁴/θ. Display (6.10) is an estimate on one global Cκ curve with its particular approximate background.

Breakdown.Periodic.r3Lambda.text: The whole-space local interactions of the compact approximation are integrated and assembled on the sequence of short intervals. The first formula of (6.9) states the corresponding factorization for a single global time curve.

Breakdown.Periodic.r3Op.text: The whole-space sequence linearization subtracts its previous-interval shift, initial-data heat contribution, and twice the interval interaction. Display (4.16) uses a global curve, and (6.14) additionally isolates a cutoff error.

Breakdown.Periodic.restrictR3Bound.text: Restriction of a whole-space velocity and its derivatives to any ball is bounded in the product of the L⁶ and L² norms, uniformly in the radius. Display (6.7) uses their sum and also states the periodic estimate.

Breakdown.Periodic.restrictTorus.text: The periodic velocity and gradient are restricted and rescaled into local L⁶ and L² data. Display (6.7) states a uniform bound directly from the homogeneous norm on the large torus.

Breakdown.Periodic.seqPerturbation.text: For normalized time intervals, a right inverse and $64\lVert R\rVert^2 C_K L^{1/4}(\rho+\lVert\xi\rVert)\le 1$ give exact mild intervals with matching endpoints. Both the datum correction and each normalized error are bounded by $2\lVert R\rVert(\rho+\lVert\xi\rVert)$, while Lemma 4.8 uses the $C^\kappa$ norm of the combined forcing $e^{t\Delta}\chi-F^a$.

Breakdown.Periodic.shellInverseTransfer.text: Two localized comparisons within $\delta$ and an explicit smallness inequality transfer a bounded whole-space right inverse to an exact periodic right inverse. Lemma 6.3 first constructs a particular approximate inverse with a defect of order $L^{-1/2}$.

Breakdown.Periodic.stepFrame.text: At scale 0<μ≤1, the heat operator is evaluated at μt and the bilinear interaction is rescaled on the unit torus. Display (3.21) also changes the spatial period and uses the homogeneous norm.

Breakdown.Periodic.torusBlowup_of_parts.text: The conclusion supplies a smooth periodic solenoidal datum and a mild trajectory whose inhomogeneous H¹ norm is unbounded on [0,T), for some T>0. Proposition 2.2 additionally gives T≤1, the two-sided rate, and local convergence to the profile.

Breakdown.Periodic.torusLambda.text: The scaled periodic local interactions of the compact approximation are integrated and assembled on short intervals. The second formula of (6.9) states the corresponding factorization for a global curve on a large torus.

Breakdown.Periodic.torusOp.text: The periodic sequence linearization subtracts its previous-interval shift, initial-data heat contribution, and twice the interaction on each normalized interval. Display (6.6) combines these in one global weighted trajectory.

Breakdown.Periodic.transplantNorm.text: The rescaled transplant has squared norm ∫|∇g|²+μ∫|g|² because the unit-torus norm is inhomogeneous. The equality in (6.1) concerns the homogeneous gradient norm, preserved by unscaled periodization.

Breakdown.Periodic.trigHs.text: Finite Fourier polynomials on the unit cell satisfy an L⁶ estimate using the weight 1+4π²|k|². Display (3.18) is the homogeneous Sobolev inequality for all mean-zero fields, uniformly over every period; (3.19) is a separate heat-forcing estimate.

Breakdown.Periodic.weight.text: The unit-torus Fourier norm uses 1+4π²|k|² and permits the zero mode. Displays (3.15) and (3.16) concern the homogeneous gradient norm on mean-zero fields, with a separate equivalence to H¹ at period one.

Breakdown.PeriodicInverseStatement.text: Under a finite-dimensional spectral splitting, invertibility of each short-interval operator, and a lift preserving the exceptional projection, a bounded right inverse solves the weighted sequence equations. Proposition 4.3 presents the result on the global Cκ trajectory space.

Breakdown.PeriodicSimilarityProfileExist.text: A smooth nonzero profile has a positive period and an orthogonal twist, solves the similarity equation, and satisfies uniform bounds $|\nabla^j W| \le C(1+|y|)^{-1-j}$ for $j=0,1,2$ and $|\nabla q| \le C(1+|y|)^{-3}$. The second-derivative and pressure-gradient bounds are additional written hypotheses beyond (1.3).

Breakdown.PhysicalMild.text: A smooth profile with the additional derivative and pressure-gradient decay and continuous energy-space slices gives a mild physical curve on each compact interval [0,T], 0<T<1. Proposition 4.1 also bundles nonvanishing and discrete self-similarity on [0,1).

Breakdown.PhysicalWeak.text: The scaled smooth profile obeys the divergence-free weak momentum identity at each t<1. This has the diffusion and transport pairings in (3.14), under the stated profile regularity and decay assumptions.

Breakdown.Piece.text: This is the space of continuous curves on one compact interval $[0,T]$, with its supremum norm. The global time weight $(1-t)^{1/4-\kappa}$ of (4.5) is imposed through a separate sequence rescaling.

Breakdown.PieceOperatorStatement.text: On [0,T], the bilinear Duhamel operator is bounded by 4C_K T¹⁄⁴ for T≤1, and the free heat-evolution operator has norm at most one. Lemma 4.7 expresses different, global Cκ estimates on [0,1).

Breakdown.PiecePerturbationStatement.text: On a compact interval of length at most one, a perturbation satisfying the linear-plus-quadratic equation has the given initial value and makes the sum an exact mild solution. Display (4.7) states both implications on the whole half-open lifespan.

Breakdown.PieceWeights.IsMultiplierField.text: The multiplier is characterized by the test pairing in (B.14), with finite L² norm, time periodicity and zero pairing against pressure gradients. These are the stated requirements that Mv belong to Hdiv.

Breakdown.PieceWeights.coefA.text: This gives the curl coefficient, including the positive λₚ|Ωₚ| contribution and the transport, rotation and coupling losses. The paper describes those losses after (B.16) without printing their complete formula.

Breakdown.PieceWeights.coefAA.text: This gives the gradient coefficient, including Zι−|∇²Dι|op−cw and the multiplier error terms. The full correction formula is absent from the paper's description of (B.16).

Breakdown.PieceWeights.coefB.text: This gives the velocity coefficient, including −|∇²Zι|op, the positive (1−cμ)μₚ|Ωₚ| term and its error terms. The paper prints only this leading description, so full formula agreement remains uncheckable.

Breakdown.PieceWeights.frameFreq.text: The rotating-frame frequency is 2πj/S+νj′. With (j,j′)=(2ι₂−ι₁,κι₁), this is exactly Ωₚ(ι) in (B.15).

Breakdown.PieceWeights.modeDensity.text: The density is the sum of the five coefficient-weighted squares of the Hessian, curl gradient, curl, gradient and velocity. This matches the displayed form (B.16); that agreement does not determine the coefficient corrections omitted from the paper.

Breakdown.PieceWeights.modeTerm.text: Substituting the five derivative norms of the projected mode into the quadratic density gives Iι in (B.16). The coefficient corrections are specified elsewhere in the formal definitions.

Breakdown.PieceWeights.multiplierGap.text: The expression is ⟨F,Mv⟩−c‖v‖w²−cμ‖v‖μ²−Σβᵢ⟨bᵢ,Mv⟩. Taking c=3/50 gives the left side of (B.20); the inequality for that expression is a separate assertion.

Breakdown.PieceWeights.shareHat.text: This is the amount removed from the curl-gradient coefficient by the multiplier estimates. The paper identifies that loss as part of the omitted corrections to (B.16), without giving its complete expression.

Breakdown.PotentialShape.IsPotentialSeri.text: The condition imposes polynomial joining, axis behavior and endpoint decay for the finite potential series. The paper explicitly does not print that representation, so this condition cannot be identified with the displayed analytic bounds (B.51) alone.

Breakdown.PotentialShape.PinShapeEntry.p.text: The definition constructs Φₗ from cylindrical cell data and Φ̃ₗ from the compact harmonic representation. Their regularity, support and divergence conditions are separate assumptions used to justify (B.52).

Breakdown.PotentialShape.potentialData_o.text: The theorem obtains the stronger potential decay and weak derivatives from explicit finite-series, axis and joining conditions. The paper leaves this potential representation unwritten, so only its analytic consequences can be compared directly with (B.51).

Breakdown.PotentialShape.potentialParts_.text: The result establishes the scalar, flux, pressure and compact-generator regularity facts for the finite potential representation. These provide the analytic inputs to Lemma B.12; the paper omits the detailed representation conditions.

Breakdown.ProfilePieceStatement.text: The rescaled profile intervals are mild, have matching dilated endpoints, recur under the twist every k intervals, and have a uniform upper bound inherited from the similarity orbit. The two-sided physical rate in Lemma 4.2 also uses the lower orbit bound and dilation law.

Breakdown.RestrictStatement.text: The quadratic mild equation can be restarted from any intermediate time by the heat semigroup law and adjacent-interval integration. Lemma 3.5 and (3.13) allow independent continuous factors f and h in the forcing, a larger class than the quadratic choice f=h=u.

Breakdown.SectionStatement.text: For a finite-rank projection and a dense linear class, there is a bounded lift J into that class with PᵤJ=Pᵤ. Restricting J to the exceptional range gives the compact-data correction space used in Proposition 4.3.

Breakdown.SimilarityResidual.text: The residual is ∂ₛW + W/2 + (y·∇)W/2 − ΔW + (W·∇)W + ∇q. Its vanishing is the momentum equation in (1.2); incompressibility and recurrence are separate conditions.

Breakdown.SixthPowerGradientBound.text: The inequality is written with sixth power integral raised to 1/3 and the gradient energy. At C=4/3 it is the square of the Sobolev inequality (B.45).

Breakdown.StepDataStatement.text: The right inverse acts on bounded sequences of short rescaled time intervals, returns an exceptional coordinate in a fixed finite-dimensional space, and lifts its initial correction into the chosen dense class. Proposition 4.3 writes the corresponding problem as one trajectory in Cκ([0,1);X).

Breakdown.TransferHolds.text: For every prescribed dense class of initial data and every ε>0, the formal conclusion chooses one mild solution whose datum is within ε of W(0) and whose dilated error is at most C(1−t)^κ for some κ>0. Proposition 2.1 also chooses a fixed finite-dimensional correction space and treats every sufficiently close datum; that whole family is absent from this conclusion.

Breakdown.UniqueStatement.text: Two mild solutions with the same initial value agree on their entire common interval, whether that interval is closed or half-open. This is the uniqueness part of Lemma 3.5; restarting is proved separately.

Breakdown.VarConstIntegralStatement.text: For two continuous curves on any compact interval, the Duhamel integral exists and is continuous up to both endpoints. The formal statement adds the estimate 4C_K(t−a)¹⁄⁴MN when t−a≤1, with M and N bounds for the input curves.

Breakdown.WeakProfile.mildFromGood_holds.text: Under the boundedness, measurability and almost-everywhere Duhamel identity hypotheses, the continuous Duhamel representative is a mild solution on every interior closed time interval. The identification of the bilinear term with the Leray heat kernel is a separate analytic step.

Breakdown.WeakProfile.physicalCurve.text: The curve is u(t) = D_{1/(1−t)}w(s₀ − log(1−t)); this is the coordinate change (7.40) after passing from normalized time to similarity time. The equality and boundedness of the L⁶ suprema in (7.63) need additional norm and periodicity arguments.

Breakdown.WeakProfile.physicalIdentity_o.text: The conclusion is the transformed Navier–Stokes equation after integration against test fields. Equation (7.41) instead displays separately the free operator and Laplacian change-of-variable identities, which the paper also interprets distributionally.

Breakdown.WeakProfile.varConst.text: The expression is the heat evolution of the starting value plus the bilinear Duhamel integral. With the bilinear operator identified with minus the differentiated Leray heat kernel, this is the expression on the right of (7.64).

Breakdown.WeakProfile.weakOrbitOfParts_h.text: The result turns weak-profile existence into existence of a continuous recurrent mild orbit after the listed analytic results are supplied. Proposition 7.11 additionally returns a smooth decaying profile identified with the specified input field.

Breakdown.breakdownOnSpace_of_profile.text: The paper constructs a smooth finite-time trajectory with (1.6); the formal conclusion instead gives, for every positive viscosity, compact smooth solenoidal data admitting no global smooth solution with one uniform kinetic-energy bound. The premise includes second-derivative and pressure-gradient decay, and the trajectory and its rate are absent from this conclusion.

Breakdown.contraction.text: Given a bounded right inverse for the weighted recurrence, every sufficiently small datum displacement ξ admits a correction e and a bounded sequence z solving the quadratic recurrence, with ‖e‖ ≤ C₁‖ξ‖. This is the discrete correction step, before the choices of compact spatial data, a physical trajectory, and its blow-up estimates.

Breakdown.dichotomyHolds.text: For a compact perturbation of an operator of norm at most b≤α<β, the spectral conclusion gives a commuting finite-rank projection and geometric bounds with α<r₁<r₂<β, together with surjectivity on the exceptional range. Taking α=b=exp(−S/4), β=1 and r₁<Θ<r₂ gives the two convergent series in (4.11).

Breakdown.dilateField.text: The physical dilation is $D_\mu u(x)=\sqrt{\mu}u(\sqrt{\mu}x)$, exactly as in (3.4).

Breakdown.embeddedProfileOrbit_holds.text: A smooth nonzero twisted-periodic profile, with the additional second-derivative and pressure-gradient decay, determines a continuous nonzero recurrent orbit in the energy space. Proposition 4.1 states the resulting properties directly for the physical velocity on [0,1).

Breakdown.exists_section.text: For a finite-rank projection and a dense linear class, there is a bounded lift J into that class with PᵤJ=Pᵤ. Restricting J to the exceptional range gives the compact-data correction space used in Proposition 4.3.

Breakdown.extended_certificate_breakdown.text: The conclusion excludes a global smooth bounded-energy whole-space solution for suitable compactly supported data at every positive viscosity. Corollary 7.2 also asserts the torus conclusion and retains the constructed trajectories, rates and chosen profile from Theorems 1.1 and 7.1.

Breakdown.extended_certificate_orbit_pro.text: Theorem 7.1 returns α, its period, a smooth profile and the bounds and symmetries of that same profile. This implication assumes the more restrictive certificate conditions and concludes only existence of a weak recurrent profile; its conclusion does not retain α or the bounds (7.38).

Breakdown.frozenForm.text: The quadratic form is ∫|Δu|² + ¼∫|∇u|² − ∫[(W·∇)u + (u·∇)W]·Δu, exactly the left-hand side of (7.22). Its lower bound is an additional certificate condition or theorem.

Breakdown.iterProd.text: This is the ordered product of successive short-interval linear maps. The one-period monodromy in (4.10) additionally removes the orthogonal twist after the period is assembled.

Breakdown.mildRegular_realization.text: From compact smooth solenoidal initial data, a mild curve on [0,T] has smooth velocity and pressure representatives, with bounded kinetic energy and gradient norm on that interval. Lemma 2.3 additionally states energy nonincrease throughout the lifespan and a periodic assertion.

Breakdown.mildUnique.text: Two mild solutions with the same initial value agree on their entire common interval, whether that interval is closed or half-open. This is the uniqueness part of Lemma 3.5; restarting is proved separately.

Breakdown.modeVel.text: The projection averages over one time period and a full axial rotation, using the conjugate harmonic, inverse rotation of the vector values and the factor 1/(2π). These are precisely the operations in (B.12).

Breakdown.monodromy.text: After sufficiently short intervals are composed and the twist removed, the period map differs compactly from the free product, whose norm is at most exp(−P/4). The same statement also provides inverses of the short-interval operators with norm at most 4/3.

Breakdown.orbitBound.text: Every continuous recurrent similarity orbit has one uniform upper norm bound. The upper physical rate in (4.4) follows after applying the quarter-power dilation law.

Breakdown.orbitNorm.text: A nonzero recurrent mild orbit has one strictly positive lower norm bound at every similarity time. The lower physical rate in (4.4) follows after applying the quarter-power dilation law.

Breakdown.orbitSeq.text: The weighted recurrence is $x_{n+1}=\theta^{-1}(Mx_n+c_n)$. Display (4.14) writes the corresponding unweighted recurrence and also identifies its continuous-time trajectory and forcing.

Breakdown.periodPairing.text: The pairing integrates F·G over space and one unit time period, exactly ⟨F,G⟩_H in (7.31). It does not subtract the frame column; that belongs to the separate forcing-to-adjoint discrepancy.

Breakdown.periodicInverse.text: Under a finite-dimensional spectral splitting, invertibility of each short-interval operator, and a lift preserving the exceptional projection, a bounded right inverse solves the weighted sequence equations. Proposition 4.3 presents the result on the global Cκ trajectory space.

Breakdown.physicalField.text: The physical curve is $D_{(1-t)^{-1}}W(s_0-\log(1-t))$, with final time fixed to one and arbitrary phase $s_0$. Display (1.4) allows any positive final time $T$.

Breakdown.physicalMild_unconditional.text: A smooth profile with the additional derivative and pressure-gradient decay and continuous energy-space slices gives a mild physical curve on each compact interval [0,T], 0<T<1. Proposition 4.1 also bundles nonvanishing and discrete self-similarity on [0,1).

Breakdown.pieceOperator.text: On [0,T], the bilinear Duhamel operator is bounded by 4C_K T¹⁄⁴ for T≤1, and the free heat-evolution operator has norm at most one. Lemma 4.7 expresses different, global Cκ estimates on [0,1).

Breakdown.piecePerturbation.text: On a compact interval of length at most one, a perturbation satisfying the linear-plus-quadratic equation has the given initial value and makes the sum an exact mild solution. Display (4.7) states both implications on the whole half-open lifespan.

Breakdown.pinValue.text: The functional integrates ∇v:Ξ_i over space and one unit time period, exactly ℓ_i(v) in (7.11). The matrix contraction uses the same Euclidean pairing after transposing the gradient convention consistently.

Breakdown.profilePiece.text: The rescaled profile intervals are mild, have matching dilated endpoints, recur under the twist every k intervals, and have a uniform upper bound inherited from the similarity orbit. The two-sided physical rate in Lemma 4.2 also uses the lower orbit bound and dilation law.

Breakdown.pushForward.text: The orthogonal action is $\rho_R u(x)=Ru(R^{-1}x)$, exactly as in (3.4), including reflections.

Breakdown.restrict.text: The quadratic mild equation can be restarted from any intermediate time by the heat semigroup law and adjacent-interval integration. Lemma 3.5 and (3.13) allow independent continuous factors f and h in the forcing, a larger class than the quadratic choice f=h=u.

Breakdown.rowNorm.text: The weighted Euclidean norm of pairings with orthonormal fields represents the paper’s unweighted norm of pairings with orthogonal fields. Absorbing $\sqrt{\tau_j}$ into the $j$th field identifies the quantities, while the supplied field normalization differs.

Breakdown.sigmaSimilarityIntegrand.text: The expression is the similarity equation tested against a solenoidal space-time field, with time coefficient 1/S and the spatial derivatives transferred by integration by parts. Pressure disappears from this weak equation, while (7.1) displays it explicitly.

Breakdown.sixthPowerGradientBound_four_t.text: The theorem states $\lVert u\rVert_{L^6}^2\le(4/3)\lVert\nabla u\rVert_{L^2}^2$ for an $L^6$ field with $L^2$ weak gradient. Taking square roots gives (B.45) with constant $2/\sqrt{3}$.

Breakdown.stationaryEnergy.text: The one-time energy is ∫|Δu|² + ∫w|∇u|², exactly |u|²_w in (7.14). The forcing-coefficient weight ω belongs to the separate norm of a pair.

Breakdown.stepData.text: The right inverse acts on bounded sequences of short rescaled time intervals, returns an exceptional coordinate in a fixed finite-dimensional space, and lifts its initial correction into the chosen dense class. Proposition 4.3 writes the corresponding problem as one trajectory in Cκ([0,1);X).

Breakdown.stepMap.text: A short-interval step sends initial data through free evolution, the inverse of the interval linearization, and endpoint evaluation. The monodromy in (4.10) composes all such steps in a period and removes the twist.

Breakdown.stretchForm.text: The stretching expression has the negative strain-curl square, the vorticity-gradient coupling and the final cross-product term with coefficient 1/2. Its signs and contractions agree with (B.18).

Breakdown.supBoundFactor.text: The constant simplifies to $(4\pi\sqrt{w_*})^{-1/2}$, exactly $c_w$ in (7.15), when $w_* > 0$.

Breakdown.transferHolds_of_dichotomy.text: For every prescribed dense class of initial data and every ε>0, the formal conclusion chooses one mild solution whose datum is within ε of W(0) and whose dilated error is at most C(1−t)^κ for some κ>0. Proposition 2.1 also chooses a fixed finite-dimensional correction space and treats every sufficiently close datum; that whole family is absent from this conclusion.

Breakdown.varConstIntegral.text: For two continuous curves on any compact interval, the Duhamel integral exists and is continuous up to both endpoints. The formal statement adds the estimate 4C_K(t−a)¹⁄⁴MN when t−a≤1, with M and N bounds for the input curves.

Breakdown.weakDefectField.text: The expression includes $T_S W$, convection, forcing and a supplied pressure-gradient field, with the Laplacian given by a chosen weak Hessian. Setting the forcing to zero and identifying that Hessian and pressure gradient recovers the strong expression in (7.1).

Breakdown.weightedEnergy.text: The energy is ∫₀¹∫(|Δv|² + w|∇v|²), exactly ‖v‖²_w in (7.14) on the admissible finite-energy class. It contains no forcing-coefficient term.

Breakdown.FarField.heatConv.text: The displayed integral is convolution with the Gaussian heat kernel. It describes the positive-time formula in (2.1); the identity at time zero is supplied by the heat semigroup, separately.

Breakdown.FarField.HeatVelocity.text: For positive time, the reconstructed velocity of the heat evolution equals Gaussian convolution almost everywhere for each element of X. Display (2.1) defines heat evolution on every Lᵖ space, including the identity convention at time zero.

Breakdown.FarField.heatVelocity_of_heatC.text: For positive time, the reconstructed velocity of the heat evolution equals Gaussian convolution almost everywhere for each element of X. Display (2.1) defines heat evolution on every Lᵖ space, including the identity convention at time zero.

Breakdown.FarField.lerayKernel.text: The kernel is the first spatial derivative of the projected heat kernel, expressed through a Gaussian derivative and an integral of third Gaussian derivatives. The estimates for every derivative order in (3.9) are a separate assertion.

Breakdown.FarField.LerayKernelBound.text: The formal bound is $|\partial_k(O_\tau)_{ij}(x)| \le C(|x|+\sqrt{\tau})^{-4}$ for positive $\tau$. Display (3.9) gives the corresponding estimate for every spatial derivative order, so this is the first-derivative case used for the bilinear convolution.

Breakdown.FarField.lerayKernelBound_hold.text: The formal bound is $|\partial_k(O_\tau)_{ij}(x)| \le C(|x|+\sqrt{\tau})^{-4}$ for positive $\tau$. Display (3.9) gives the corresponding estimate for every spatial derivative order, so this is the first-derivative case used for the bilinear convolution.

Breakdown.FarField.BilinTestKernel.text: For a compact smooth solenoidal field, the diagonal bilinear term equals the representation of −∇Oτ∗(u⊗u). Display (3.10) ranges over arbitrary inputs in X and also over general tensor divergences.

Breakdown.FarField.BilinKernel.text: For each positive time and each u∈X, the physical velocity of K(τ)(u,u) equals −∇Oτ∗(u⊗u) almost everywhere. Display (3.10) also states the distinct-input formula and the identity for a general tensor divergence; polarization recovers the former, while the latter is a separate assertion.

Breakdown.FarField.bilinKernel_of_test_d.text: For each positive time and each u∈X, the physical velocity of K(τ)(u,u) equals −∇Oτ∗(u⊗u) almost everywhere. Display (3.10) also states the distinct-input formula and the identity for a general tensor divergence; polarization recovers the former, while the latter is a separate assertion.

Breakdown.Periodic.ShellTorus.Internal.s.text: Compactly supported $L^2$ forcing transplanted to the unit torus satisfies $C\mu^{1/4}\tau^{-3/4}\lVert A\rVert_{L^{3/2}}$ when the support fits the scaled cell and $\mu\tau\le 1$. Display (3.19) treats all mean-zero $L^{3/2}$ forcing at every period and positive time.

Breakdown.Periodic.sourceOp.text: This is the bounded map taking an $L^2$ whole-space source to its projected, heat-evolved periodic transplant. The particular $\tau^{-3/4}$ estimate is a further theorem, under compact-support and scale assumptions.

Breakdown.Cert.Internal.FreeEnergyLocal..text: The condition describes a continuous periodic energy-space curve for the constructed free solution and its interval-integrated energy identity in similarity time. Equation (7.45) instead concerns the physical-time gradient energy of a general admissible trajectory.

Breakdown.Freq.VelocityDilate.text: The assertion identifies the velocity of a dilated energy-space field with its physical dilation, almost everywhere in space. It does not state the equality or boundedness of the time-weighted L⁶ suprema in (7.63).

Breakdown.Freq.velocityCov_holds.text: The result proves covariance of physical velocity under orthogonal transformations and positive dilation. Equation (7.63) additionally uses the exact L⁶ scaling and the continuous periodic profile to bound the physical-time supremum.

Breakdown.FarField.IsRegularOrbitField.text: The hypotheses require a smooth recurrent solution with uniform derivatives through order three, a vanishing tail, an L² pressure gradient and the profile integral equation. They are intermediate assumptions for the separate decay argument, not the original weak-field assumptions of Proposition 7.11.

Breakdown.FarField.IsSmoothOrbitField.text: The conditions require a smooth recurrent solution, uniform derivatives through order three, a vanishing spatial tail and an L² pressure gradient. The profile integral equation is a further condition in the decay argument and is absent here.

Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.Internal.Rem.text: Equation (C.1) states the complete curl-cross similarity equation. This result is the algebraic identity relating the derivative, curl-cross term and transposed derivative pairing; it supplies one component of that equation and contains no numerical iteration.

Breakdown.Coercive.Internal.TestDensityP.text: Equation (C.1) contains the full self-similar evolution. This identity only gives −Δφ=curl(curl φ)−∇div φ for smooth fields, which supplies its diffusion term when the field is solenoidal.

Breakdown.CertCell.CellCalculus.coupling.text: Equation (C.2) gives the full linearized similarity operator. The linked formula contains its two curl-cross convection terms, (curl v)×W+(curl W)×v, with the derivative of v supplied separately.

Breakdown.CertCell.CellCalculus.IsStrong.text: Equation (C.2) gives the Newton linearization. The formal condition writes an almost-everywhere right-hand-side identity with separate time-and-drift, second-derivative and pressure data and an actuator sum, so identifying it with that operator requires those additional identifications.

Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.remainderAnn.text: The surrounding text of (C.2) describes a matrix-free Newton computation. This theorem gives a continuum weak-testing identity under the stated derivative and right-hand-side conditions; it does not check the numerical iteration.

families.name: From a certificate to a profile
From cell data to the certificate

topics.name: The blow-up statements
topics.description: Smooth solutions, breakdown on space and on the torus, and the theorems that state them (Theorem 1.1, Theorem 7.1).

topics.name: The fractional extension
topics.description: The authors' separate extension with dissipation exponent between 1 and 5/4, outside the classical paper.

topics.name: Heat flow and mild solutions
topics.description: The heat semigroup, the bilinear Duhamel term, mild solutions, restarting and uniqueness (§3).

topics.name: Recurrent profiles
topics.description: Self-similar time-periodic profiles, their slices and orbits, and weak profiles read as physical fields (§2, §4.1, §7.11).

topics.name: Monodromy and the correction
topics.description: The period map, its compact-plus-small splitting, the spectral projection and the fixed point that corrects a profile to an exact solution (§4).

topics.name: Passing to the torus
topics.description: The solenoidal cutoff, periodization and the periodic right inverse that move the construction onto the torus (§5–6).

topics.name: From certificate to profile
topics.description: Certificate data, the free operator, convection, held solutions and the smoothing of the weak profile they produce (§7).

topics.name: The coercive multiplier estimate
topics.description: The multiplier, its five density coefficients and lower bound, and the a priori estimate it gives (Appendix B.1 and B.2).

topics.name: Encoded cell data
topics.description: The finitely represented inputs: coordinates and harmonics, the profile representation, splines and jets, physical cells, rows, weights and potentials.

topics.name: Reduction to the quarter plane
topics.description: Symmetry reduction of the density to the meridian quarter plane (B.3).

topics.name: Cells, traces and tails
topics.description: Integrability, the common vector of unknowns, resolved modes, the tail budget and the exterior estimate (B.4).

topics.name: Angular and ray-exterior tests
topics.description: The angular inequalities, the pointwise test and the integrated test on ray exteriors (B.5 and B.6).

topics.name: The matrix tree lower bound
topics.description: The tree conditions on the cell matrices and the passage from all cells to the global inequality (B.7 and B.8).

topics.name: Changing the profile
topics.description: Bounds for moving estimates from the reference field to the actual profile (B.9).

topics.name: The adjoint pairing and its error
topics.description: The quadratic adjoint pairing, the azimuthal dual norm and the linear adjoint error with potentials and pins (B.10 to B.12).

topics.name: The offset and the certificate
topics.description: Enclosing the constant, linear and quadratic offset, and the fifteen fields of CellSystemCondition that make the data a certificate (B.13 and B.14).
